headline: Ghalibaf says Americans have voted ‘no to war’ after Republican losses in Congress
description: Iranian Parliament Speaker Mohammad Baqer Ghalibaf has said Americans have voted “no to war” following Republican...
article_text:
Iranian Parliament Speaker Mohammad Baqer Ghalibaf has said Americans have voted “no to war” following Republican losses in both chambers of Congress.

“Conscience or the cost of living, Americans said NO TO WAR, and we endorse this message,” Ghalibaf said in a post on X.

He warned that if the US government betrayed the public’s will to serve “international paymasters and blackmailers”, it would “learn our NO comes with a Nightmare”.

headline: Fazl hints at launching street agitation
description: Says JUI-F will not allow govt to "plunder" natural resources.
author: Nisar Ahmad Khan
article_text:
MANSEHRA: Jamiat Ulema-i-Islam-Fazl chief Maulana Fazlur Rahman said here on Tuesday that his party would never allow the government to plunder the natural resources and deprive people of their democratic rights in the country.

“The government wants to divide the nation and create conflict to plunder natural resources. We will never allow it to undermine democracy, politics and rights of people. JUI-F stands firm against such anti-people policies and actions,” he told a workers convention, hinting at launching a street agitation.

Malik Waheed, former divisional president of Pakistan Peoples Party in Hazara, announced his decision to join JUI-F on the occasion after parting ways with PPP.

Maulana Fazlur Rahman urged charged workers to stand firmly with him as he prepared to launch a street agitation. “I see you as the strongest force in the country.

Says JUI-F will not allow govt to plunder natural resources

You must stand firm against oppression and adversity, as activists of no other party dare to stand up at this critical juncture,” he said.

He said that JUI-F was the only political force playing the role of a genuine opposition by raising its voice inside and outside parliament against what he called illegal centres of power, anti-national policies and interference of foreign powers.

“We will not allow anyone to plunder Khyber Pakhtunkhwa in the name of terrorism. The province’s natural resources belong equally to its indigenous communities,” he said.

The JUI-F chief questioned the effectiveness of successive governments’ counterterrorism policies, saying billions of dollars had been received for the fight against terrorism and 13 operations had been conducted since 2010, yet militancy continued to increase and innocent people were being killed.

He said that people were the custodians and owners of country’s resources, but those questioning the government’s performance were subjected to character assassination.

Mr Rahman said that the government shouldn’t consider his party to compromise on its principles and deviate from its stance on the enforcement of true democracy in the country, particularly in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa.

JUI-F provincial chief Maulana Attaur Rahman said on the occasion that his party would not accept revival of the status of former Federally Administered Tribal Areas (Fata) without taking tribesmen into confidence.

“PPP and PML-N are two faces of the same coin, as both have been playing in the hands of establishment. They first changed the tribal status of Fata and now reversed it without taking indigenous people into confidence,” he said.

Maulana Ajmal Khan, JUI-F general secretary in Punjab, condemned the reported drone flight over Maulana Fazlur Rahman’s residence and called for an immediate end to such acts.

He said that the government shouldn’t cross its limits to compel JUI-F workers to come forward for the security of Maulana Fazlur Rahman.

“We don’t want to take law into our hands. This is why we are peaceful, but we want to make it clear that we wouldn’t tolerate any attack on the dignity of our leaders’ honour through such immoral acts of propagating against him and his family members,” he said.

Speaking on the occasion, provincial office-bearers of JUI-F Maulana Nasir Mehmood, Malik Waheed and Malik Naveed said that workers of the party were ready to stand shoulder to shoulder with their leader Maulana Fazlur Rahman in his fight for the rights of people.

Published in Dawn, November 4th, 2026

headline: Seminary teacher held for beating student to death in KP's Bajaur
description: The teacher had fled after allegedly beating his student to death inside the madressah, officials say.
author: Our Correspondent
article_text:
BAJAUR: Police have arrested a seminary teacher for allegedly beating a student to death in Bajaur district, officials said on Tuesday.

They added that the teacher of a seminary in the Qazafi Bandagi area of Utmankhel tehsil, who had fled after allegedly beating his student to death inside the madressah, was arrested during a raid conducted after the incident came to light.

Taking notice of the death of a 12-year-old child, Regional Police Officer, Malakand Division, Zahid Nawaz ordered the arrest of the suspect. A team from Utmankhel police station, led by District Police Officer Khan Zeb Mohmand, arrested him during a raid, according to a statement.

The statement said that the raiding party led by SHO Utmankhel police station Mustafa Kamal arrested the suspect at a place where he had fled after committing the crime. The suspect had been shifted to the police station for legal proceedings after a first information report (FIR) was registered against him under Section 302 of the Pakistan Penal Code.

An investigation into the tragic incident was underway to ensure the suspect was punished as per the law.

“The death of an innocent child at the hands of his teacher inside a seminary is a tragic and horrific incident. The police stand with the bereaved family in this difficult time to ensure immediate justice for them,” the statement quoted the DPO as saying.

According to the FIR, the body of the deceased, identified as Arshad, a resident of the Mandal area of Salarzai tehsil, was found inside the mosque/seminary.

The suspect had been shifted to the police station for legal proceedings after a first information report (FIR) was registered against him under Section 302 of the Pakistan Penal Code.
An investigation into the tragic incident was underway to ensure the suspect was punished as per the law.

“The death of an innocent child at the hands of his teacher inside a seminary is a tragic and horrific incident. The police stand with the bereaved family in this difficult time to ensure immediate justice for them,” the statement quoted the DPO as saying.

headline: Teachers in Peshawar protest ‘abrupt layoffs’ by UNHCR
description: As many as 291 teachers, providing education to Afghan children for the past 35 to 40 years, have been laid off without prior notice or any financial relief.
author: Bureau Report
article_text:
PESHAWAR: Hundreds of Pakistani teachers, who provided education to Afghan children in refugee camps for decades, but were laid off without any financial relief, protested here on Tuesday against the ‘abrupt’ layoffs.

As many as 291 teachers, who have been providing education to Afghan children under the auspices of the United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees (UNHCR) for the past 35 to 40 years, have been laid off without prior notice or any financial relief.

The affected teachers, including 100 men and 191 women, were reportedly dismissed from service on Oct 31. They belong to Peshawar, Mardan, Timergara, Nowshera, Swabi, Haripur, Kohat, Dera Ismail Khan, Bannu, Lakki Marwat, Hangu, Tall, Chakdara, and Jalala Shergarh.

The dismissed teachers demanded compensation and financial relief for their decades of service.

The protest was led by Tufail Ahmed and Farhana Durrani, who heads the women teachers. Addressing the protesters, Mr Ahmed said they had devoted nearly four decades of their lives to educating Afghan children in refugee camps but had been dismissed through a single administrative decision without any notice or relief.

He said the teachers had already been deprived of medical allowances, other financial benefits and gratuity despite serving in schools established in Afghan refugee camps for decades.

“We served the institution for four decades, but were sent home at the stroke of a pen without any compensation or relief,” he said.

On the occasion, Ms Durrani said she had spent 35 years teaching Afghan children and had worked tirelessly to fulfil her responsibilities.

“After 35 years of dedicated service, the UNHCR sent us home through a single phone call, without providing any financial relief,” she said.

The protesters said the sudden termination of their employment had pushed hundreds of families into severe financial difficulties, with many struggling to meet even their basic household expenses.

They complained that despite repeatedly visiting the UNHCR office to present their grievances, no official was willing to hear them or engage in dialogue.

They further alleged that instead of addressing their concerns, the office had closed its doors to them and deployed police personnel outside, with protesters being warned of a possible baton charge.

They appealed to Khyber Pakhtunkhwa Governor Faisal Karim Kundi to intervene and play his role in securing relief for the affected teachers and their families.

A large number of young and elderly women teachers also participated in the sit-in, demanding recognition of their decades-long services and financial assistance following their dismissal.

Published in Dawn, November 4th, 2026

headline: New IO given 10 days to complete Mir Raza murder probe
description: Court directives come on IO's application stating he had received a case file containing more than 1,100 pages and needed more time to complete the investigation.
author: The Newspaper's Staff Reporter
article_text:
KARACHI: A judicial magistrate on Tuesday granted an additional 10 days to the newly appointed investigation officer (IO) to complete the probe into the Mir Raza murder case.

A day earlier, the court had issued a show-cause notice to the head of the joint investigation team (JIT), police officer Irfan Baloch, and sought his response over the police failure to submit the final charge sheet in the case.

On Tuesday, co-opted IO DSP Fareed Ahmed Khan filed an application before the judicial magistrate (East), seeking an additional 14 days to complete the investigation.

In the application, the DSP informed the court that he had been appointed as a co-opted investigation officer in the case and had received a case file containing more than 1,100 pages.

He added that the JIT was formed to investigate the case thoroughly.

After hearing the investigation officer, the court granted him an additional 10 days to complete the probe.

The 25-year-old businessman, Mir Raza, had gone missing on July 28 after leaving his home in PECHS.

His body, bearing a through-and-through gunshot wound, was found in bushes in Gulistan-i-Jauhar a day later.

The Sindh home department had formed the JIT, led by DIG Irfan Baloch, on the recommendation of a single-member judicial commission comprising Justice Omar Sial of the Sindh High Court.

The team was tasked with investigating the circumstances surrounding Mir Raza’s death and possible negligence in the case.

Two previous high-level investigation teams had failed to identify the culprit or establish how Mir Raza’s body came to be found in mysterious circumstances.

Published in Dawn, November 4th, 2026

headline: Nasa's Swift satellite telescope heads for fiery re-entry 22 years after launch
description: The observatory, which has no onboard propulsion system of its own, has been drifting toward an expected demise for months as it circles the globe at a speed of roughly 17,000 miles per houR.
author: Reuters
article_text:
An aging Nasa satellite telescope that a robotic spacecraft was sent to retrieve on a failed rescue mission this summer was headed for a fiery re-entry into Earth’s atmosphere on Wednesday, nearly 22 years after it was launched into orbit.

The Neil Gehrels Swift Observatory, weighing roughly 3,200 pounds (1,452 kg), was set to tumble out of orbit and burn up in the atmosphere somewhere over the tropics, with fragments surviving re-entry unlikely to threaten populated areas, according to Nasa.

The US Space Force has put the odds of harm coming to anyone on Earth at one chance in 2,100, Nasa said in an online statement, projecting the time of re-entry at approximately 3:30am EST (0830 GMT). The Aerospace Corporation, a nonprofit national security research entity, projected a re-entry window of 5:19am EST, plus or minus two hours.

London-based astrophysicist Jonathan McDowell, an honorary professor at the Durham University Space Research Centre, cited revised US Space Force data predicting re-entry most likely to come around 7:45am EST.

“The satellite is in a very circular orbit, skimming the top of the atmosphere,” he told Reuters by phone on Tuesday night. “The question is at what point does it heat up enough that it starts breaking up.” Nasa’s prized $500 million Swift satellite, a first-of-its-kind multi-wavelength space observatory, has been studying gamma-ray bursts and other cosmic phenomena since 2004, using its array of three telescopes.

The observatory, which has no onboard propulsion system of its own, has been drifting toward an expected demise for months as it circles the globe at a speed of roughly 17,000 miles per hour (27,359 kph).

Astronomers had hoped to extend Swift’s mission for a number of years by giving the satellite telescope a lift.

In July, Nasa and Arizona-based startup Katalyst launched a specially built rescue vehicle called LINK on a mission to rendezvous with Swift, latch onto the satellite and tug the observatory back into a higher, more sustainable orbit.

But the LINK spacecraft itself began spinning uncontrollably soon after reaching space, and by mid-August, mission managers abandoned the effort, resigned to letting Swift continue to meet its fate.

The aborted rescue attempt, the first US mission of its kind, took on heightened significance as a demonstration of a new orbital grappling technology seen as pivotal to the outcome of the US-China space race.

The LINK effort was closely watched as a trial run of a key satellite-maintenance technology with potential dual-use military space applications.

Katalyst touted the mission as a historic endeavor that designed, built and tested the LINK rescue vehicle on an unprecedented nine-month production schedule under a $30 million Nasa contract.

Swift was launched more than two decades ago to explore the most powerful known explosions in the universe, bursts of gamma-ray radiation emanating from the cores of distant galaxies.

Originally designed for a two-year prime mission, Swift remained in operation far longer with observations of a wide range of cosmic objects, from galaxies powered by supermassive black holes and stars emitting X-ray flares, to comets and asteroids streaking through our own solar system.

article_html:
An aging Nasa satellite telescope that a robotic spacecraft was sent to retrieve on a failed rescue mission this summer was headed for a fiery re-entry into Earth’s atmosphere on Wednesday, nearly 22 years after it was launched into orbit.

The Neil Gehrels Swift Observatory, weighing roughly 3,200 pounds (1,452 kg), was set to tumble out of orbit and burn up in the atmosphere somewhere over the tropics, with fragments surviving re-entry unlikely to threaten populated areas, according to Nasa.

The US Space Force has put the odds of harm coming to anyone on Earth at one chance in 2,100, Nasa said in an online statement, projecting the time of re-entry at approximately 3:30am EST (0830 GMT). The Aerospace Corporation, a nonprofit national security research entity, projected a re-entry window of 5:19am EST, plus or minus two hours.

London-based astrophysicist Jonathan McDowell, an honorary professor at the Durham University Space Research Centre, cited revised US Space Force data predicting re-entry most likely to come around 7:45am EST.

“The satellite is in a very circular orbit, skimming the top of the atmosphere,” he told Reuters by phone on Tuesday night. “The question is at what point does it heat up enough that it starts breaking up.” Nasa’s prized $500 million Swift satellite, a first-of-its-kind multi-wavelength space observatory, has been studying gamma-ray bursts and other cosmic phenomena since 2004, using its array of three telescopes.

The observatory, which has no onboard propulsion system of its own, has been drifting toward an expected demise for months as it circles the globe at a speed of roughly 17,000 miles per hour (27,359 kph).

Astronomers had hoped to extend Swift’s mission for a number of years by giving the satellite telescope a lift.

In July, Nasa and Arizona-based startup Katalyst launched a specially built rescue vehicle called LINK on a mission to rendezvous with Swift, latch onto the satellite and tug the observatory back into a higher, more sustainable orbit.

But the LINK spacecraft itself began spinning uncontrollably soon after reaching space, and by mid-August, mission managers abandoned the effort, resigned to letting Swift continue to meet its fate.

The aborted rescue attempt, the first US mission of its kind, took on heightened significance as a demonstration of a new orbital grappling technology seen as pivotal to the outcome of the US-China space race.

The LINK effort was closely watched as a trial run of a key satellite-maintenance technology with potential dual-use military space applications.

Katalyst touted the mission as a historic endeavor that designed, built and tested the LINK rescue vehicle on an unprecedented nine-month production schedule under a $30 million Nasa contract.

Swift was launched more than two decades ago to explore the most powerful known explosions in the universe, bursts of gamma-ray radiation emanating from the cores of distant galaxies.

Originally designed for a two-year prime mission, Swift remained in operation far longer with observations of a wide range of cosmic objects, from galaxies powered by supermassive black holes and stars emitting X-ray flares, to comets and asteroids streaking through our own solar system.

headline: Lone Star turns blue: Democrats Talarico, Hinojosa topple Texas Republicans
description: The result was a major setback for Trump, who threw his weight behind Ken Paxton and made Texas a campaign priority.
author: AFP
article_text:
Democrat James Talarico, a former schoolteacher and Presbyterian seminarian who campaigned on a “politics of love,” on Tuesday won the US Senate race in Texas, dealing a historic blow to Republicans that could reshape American politics.

Talarico defeated the state’s attorney general Ken Paxton, a close ally of President Donald Trump who was heavily backed by tech billionaire Elon Musk, US media projected.

The result was a major setback for Trump, who threw his weight behind Paxton and made the state a campaign priority.

“We defeated Goliath,” Talarico told a victory rally in Austin, the state capital.

“In this race, we went up against our own Goliaths. The richest man in the world, the most powerful man in the world, and the entire Washington, DC establishment,” he said.

Talarico took aim at billionaires “who own the social media algorithms, who own the cable news networks, who own the politicians fighting on our screens” and who “want us at each other’s throats.”

In another political earthquake for the deeply conservative southern border state, Democrat Gina Hinojosa unseated incumbent Texas Governor Greg Abbott.

Talarico and Hinojosa are the first Democrats to win statewide office in Texas since 1994.

Hinojosa, a 52-year-old attorney and state lawmaker, is part of a new generation of Democrats who are seeking to attract independents and voters disillusioned by Trump’s unpopular war in the Middle East and skyrocketing prices for gas and everyday goods.

Thousands of supporters gathered at a watch party in Austin erupted in joy as the results came in, many of them crying and hugging.

Some chanted “Si se puede” (“Yes we can” in Spanish), while drivers passing by honked their horns in celebration.

“It’s a huge win for Texas, but it’s a giant win for the United States, having James Talarico in the Senate to try to wrest control of this government that’s out of control,” said Kathy Jackoway, an Austin resident in her 60s.

“Everybody is suffering. Everybody is hurting, and Trump is busy building monuments to himself.”

Anisha, 29, said she hoped the two Democrats would govern “for everyone, not just the billionaires, not just the elite.”

‘Mandate the size of Texas’

The landmark victories for Democrats could signal that Texas, the country’s second most populous state with 40 electoral votes, is becoming competitive in national elections, a shift that could reshape the electoral map for future races.

“This is a win the size of Texas and now we have a mandate the size of Texas,” Talarico said.

The results mark a bruising defeat for Musk, who spent more than $200 million to support Talarico’s rival, according to federal filings.

The world’s richest man, Musk has moved the headquarters of Tesla, SpaceX and X to Texas.

The spread of AI data centres across Texas became a central issue in both races, as residents worried about rising electricity bills, water use and strain on the power grid.

Talarico and Hinojosa both called for tighter regulation, prompting Abbott, a longtime champion of the industry, to propose new rules of his own.

Talarico ran on a blend of Christian faith and economic populism, describing the contest as a David versus Goliath fight and inviting Republicans dissatisfied with the party to join him.

Trump traveled to Texas four times in the month before the election to rally for Paxton, whom he endorsed over four-term incumbent senator John Cornyn in the Republican primary.

Talarico, 37, was elected to the Texas House of Representatives in 2018 and built a national following with speeches combining progressive politics, biblical teaching and criticism of wealthy elites.

He defeated congresswoman Jasmine Crockett in the Democratic primary and sought to broaden his appeal by criticising aspects of former president Joe Biden’s immigration policies.

Paxton, 63, survived impeachment by the Republican-controlled Texas House in 2023 on allegations of corruption and abuse of power before being acquitted by the state Senate. He has denied wrongdoing.

During the campaign, Talarico drew support from voters who had left the Republican Party, as well as from younger voters.

Talarico took aim at billionaires “who own the social media algorithms, who own the cable news networks, who own the politicians fighting on our screens” and who “want us at each other’s throats.”

In another political earthquake for the deeply conservative southern border state, Democrat Gina Hinojosa unseated incumbent Texas Governor Greg Abbott.

Talarico and Hinojosa are the first Democrats to win statewide office in Texas since 1994.

Hinojosa, a 52-year-old attorney and state lawmaker, is part of a new generation of Democrats who are seeking to attract independents and voters disillusioned by Trump’s unpopular war in the Middle East and skyrocketing prices for gas and everyday goods.

Thousands of supporters gathered at a watch party in Austin erupted in joy as the results came in, many of them crying and hugging.

Some chanted “Si se puede” (“Yes we can” in Spanish), while drivers passing by honked their horns in celebration.

“It’s a huge win for Texas, but it’s a giant win for the United States, having James Talarico in the Senate to try to wrest control of this government that’s out of control,” said Kathy Jackoway, an Austin resident in her 60s.

“Everybody is suffering. Everybody is hurting, and Trump is busy building monuments to himself.”

Anisha, 29, said she hoped the two Democrats would govern “for everyone, not just the billionaires, not just the elite.”

The landmark victories for Democrats could signal that Texas, the country’s second most populous state with 40 electoral votes, is becoming competitive in national elections, a shift that could reshape the electoral map for future races.

“This is a win the size of Texas and now we have a mandate the size of Texas,” Talarico said.

The results mark a bruising defeat for Musk, who spent more than $200 million to support Talarico’s rival, according to federal filings.

The world’s richest man, Musk has moved the headquarters of Tesla, SpaceX and X to Texas.

The spread of AI data centres across Texas became a central issue in both races, as residents worried about rising electricity bills, water use and strain on the power grid.

Talarico and Hinojosa both called for tighter regulation, prompting Abbott, a longtime champion of the industry, to propose new rules of his own.

Talarico ran on a blend of Christian faith and economic populism, describing the contest as a David versus Goliath fight and inviting Republicans dissatisfied with the party to join him.

Trump traveled to Texas four times in the month before the election to rally for Paxton, whom he endorsed over four-term incumbent senator John Cornyn in the Republican primary.

Talarico, 37, was elected to the Texas House of Representatives in 2018 and built a national following with speeches combining progressive politics, biblical teaching and criticism of wealthy elites.

He defeated congresswoman Jasmine Crockett in the Democratic primary and sought to broaden his appeal by criticising aspects of former president Joe Biden’s immigration policies.

Paxton, 63, survived impeachment by the Republican-controlled Texas House in 2023 on allegations of corruption and abuse of power before being acquitted by the state Senate. He has denied wrongdoing.

During the campaign, Talarico drew support from voters who had left the Republican Party, as well as from younger voters.

headline: Pakistan's Maliha Ali topples Russia's Drozdova at MMA world championships
description: Maliha secured the first two rounds using strong cage control and ground strikes, and managed to fend off a late takedown attempt in the match.
author: Ahmed Ali
article_text:
Russia arrived at the IMMAF World Championships in Tbilisi, Georgia, with more than 60 athletes, government backing and one of the best-funded programmes in the sport. On Tuesday, a 24-year-old from Hunza, Gilgit-Baltistan, beat one of them.

Maliha Ali defeated Veronika Drozdova, a two-time European champion and, at 19, by split decision in their featherweight (65.8kg) bout at the world championships of amateur mixed martial arts.

Maliha, who is also a wushu champion and a national kickboxing gold medallist, came into the tournament off a silver medal at the IMMAF World Cup in Angola earlier this year.

The fight was won early and nearly lost late.

Fighting from a southpaw stance, Maliha started cautiously before closing the distance and pinning the Russian against the cage. She landed clean strikes to finish the opening round strongly, though Drozdova found a couple of overhand lefts.

Maliha dominated the second. She secured a takedown, taking the fight to the floor, and moved into full mount, sitting astride her opponent’s torso, to land heavy blows from the top.

But she had spent much of her energy in those two rounds and appeared to tire in the third, where Drozdova took her down and controlled the action on the ground.

The round went to the Russian, but the first two belonged to Maliha. The judges agreed.

When the final bell rang, she stood with her arms raised, not in certainty, but in hope.

When her name was announced, Maliha let out a roar. Omar Ahmed, president of the Pakistan MMA Federation, leapt with joy from her corner.

She hugged her opponent, then dropped to the mat in prostration, the Pakistan flag draped over her shoulders: a moment of faith and gratitude after a hard-fought battle.

“I was listening to the corner and the coach’s instructions during the fight,” Maliha told Dawn. “We worked on our opponent’s game plan, how she fights, and executed our strategy. And thankfully it worked.”

Omar said the federation held a six-week camp and brought in an international jiu-jitsu and grappling coach after spotting weaknesses during Maliha’s silver-medal run in Angola earlier this year.

“There were some holes in their game which we spotted during the event in Angola,” Omar told Dawn. “The coach worked on the mistakes that she made during her previous fights, and we saw the improvement today.”

He acknowledged the disparity in resources between the two nations.

“Russia has one of the most well-funded MMA programs,” Omar said. “Compared to them, we are the most underfunded and probably the least-resourced federation competing in this event because of the sports policy in Pakistan. But still, we manage to eke out victories against such formidable opponents.”

For Omar, each victory against the odds carries a deeper meaning.

“Watching our fighters win against such tough opponents brings me joy which I cannot put into words,” he added. “We come from almost nothing; the only thing we have is our grit and desire to succeed, and I guess that’s what matters at the end of the day.”

It is a familiar position for the federation. Pakistan’s campaign at last year’s championships, also held in Tbilisi, was reported to be entirely self-funded through private sponsorship, with no government money.

Maliha faces Mexico’s Andrea Gabriela Guzman Salazar in the quarter-finals on Wednesday. Her twin sister Manesha, who won gold in Luanda earlier this year, fights Poland’s Martyna Caruk on the same day. Both are chasing world titles.

headline: Democratic takeover of US Congress: What happens next
description: Emboldened by victories deep in traditional Republican territory, the party is promising swift action on living costs and the war in Iran, while signalling that investigations of alleged abuses and corruption will be a major priority.
author: AFP
article_text:
Democrats are preparing a legislative offensive against US President Donald Trump after their sweeping midterm victory handed them control of both chambers of Congress and the power to challenge his policies, investigate his administration and block his nominees.

Emboldened by victories deep in traditional Republican territory, the party is promising swift action on living costs and the war in Iran, while signalling that investigations of alleged abuses and corruption will be a major priority.

House Democratic leader Hakeem Jeffries, who is in line to become the first Black speaker when the new Congress takes office in January, vowed to go after what he described as “unprecedented corruption” in the government.

“Because if you have people in high office who are so focused on enriching themselves, their family members, their friends, or their donors, then they’re not focused on making life better for the American people,” he said.

But Democrats will not have a free hand. Trump retains his veto, while Senate rules allow Republicans to obstruct most legislation.

Here are the opportunities — and obstacles — ahead.

First 100 hours

Jeffries has promised an ambitious legislative push in the House’s first 100 hours, focused on affordability — the issue that dominated an election shaped by tariffs, high prices and the Iran war.

His priorities include restoring expired Affordable Care Act health insurance subsidies, reversing nearly $1 trillion in Medicaid cuts enacted under Trump, rolling back tariffs and pressing for an end to the conflict, which has sent fuel costs soaring.

With majorities in both chambers, Democrats can bring their proposals to votes and take charge of spending negotiations. They could use federal budget deadlines to demand concessions, although confrontations over spending risk government shutdowns.

‘Lawyer up’

Oversight may offer an even more immediate means of challenging Trump. Robert Garcia, the Democrat expected to chair the powerful House Oversight Committee, fired off a blunt election-night message to Republicans on social media: “LAWYER UP.”

Oregon Senator Ron Wyden was even more concise, posting a single word: “Subpoenas.” With control of committees in both chambers, Democrats can summon officials, demand documents and hold public hearings, potentially putting Trump and his senior aides under intense scrutiny.

Likely subjects include the Trump family’s business and cryptocurrency dealings, government contracts involving billionaire Elon Musk, cuts to federal agencies, immigration enforcement and the conduct of the Iran war. Democrats have also signalled interest in the handling of files relating to notorious sex offender Jeffrey Epstein.

The administration could resist demands for testimony or documents, triggering court battles. Democrats could pursue Trump’s third impeachment, though party leaders have not committed to doing so. Senate muscle

The Senate majority gives Democrats another powerful lever: control of confirmations. They can block Trump’s judicial and cabinet nominees, including any selection to fill a Supreme Court vacancy, potentially curbing his influence over the courts long after he leaves office. Democratic Senate chairs will also decide which bills and investigations receive committee attention.

Trump struck a conciliatory note after the rout, praising Democrats for doing a “good job” and telling The New York Times that he would accept the result and expected to work with them. He even raised the possibility of cooperation on immigration. But he had previously warned that if Democrats won Congress, “I veto everything” — a reminder that the next two years could be defined as much by confrontation as compromise.

Democrats are preparing a legislative offensive against US President Donald Trump after their sweeping midterm victory handed them control of both chambers of Congress and the power to challenge his policies, investigate his administration and block his nominees.

Emboldened by victories deep in traditional Republican territory, the party is promising swift action on living costs and the war in Iran, while signalling that investigations of alleged abuses and corruption will be a major priority.

House Democratic leader Hakeem Jeffries, who is in line to become the first Black speaker when the new Congress takes office in January, vowed to go after what he described as “unprecedented corruption” in the government.

“Because if you have people in high office who are so focused on enriching themselves, their family members, their friends, or their donors, then they’re not focused on making life better for the American people,” he said.

But Democrats will not have a free hand. Trump retains his veto, while Senate rules allow Republicans to obstruct most legislation.

Here are the opportunities — and obstacles — ahead.

First 100 hours

Jeffries has promised an ambitious legislative push in the House’s first 100 hours, focused on affordability — the issue that dominated an election shaped by tariffs, high prices and the Iran war.

His priorities include restoring expired Affordable Care Act health insurance subsidies, reversing nearly $1 trillion in Medicaid cuts enacted under Trump, rolling back tariffs and pressing for an end to the conflict, which has sent fuel costs soaring.

With majorities in both chambers, Democrats can bring their proposals to votes and take charge of spending negotiations. They could use federal budget deadlines to demand concessions, although confrontations over spending risk government shutdowns.

‘Lawyer up’

Oversight may offer an even more immediate means of challenging Trump. Robert Garcia, the Democrat expected to chair the powerful House Oversight Committee, fired off a blunt election-night message to Republicans on social media: “LAWYER UP.”

headline: Dashain gone, Tihar uncertain: Nepali workers stranded in Saudi Arabia as Houthi attacks disrupt flights
description: Houthi attacks have disrupted nearly half of scheduled flights from Saudi airports, leaving migrant workers without clear information as their leave runs out and exit-re-entry permits near expiry.
author: ANN, The Kathmandu Post
article_text:
KATHMANDU: Rajesh Rai from Khotang was preparing to return home after three years in Saudi Arabia to celebrate Dashain with family. His employer had granted him a month’s leave and he had an exit-re-entry visa. He had booked an October 11 Air Arabia flight from Riyadh to Kathmandu via Sharjah.

But a day before departure, Houthi rebels attacked King Khalid International Airport. Thirteen people, according to Saudi authorities, were killed and more than 300 injured. The airport was shut.

After a friend told him that flights were operating from Jeddah, Rai travelled nearly 1,000 kilometres by bus for 13 hours, paying Rs7,000. But he remains in a friend’s room, unsure when he can fly home.

“I am neither in my company’s camp nor have I been able to reach home,” said Rai.

“Dashain has passed, Tihar is around the corner and my leave is about to end.”

Rai is among hundreds of Nepali workers whose plans to return home have been thrown into uncertainty. Between October 8 and 25, about 45 per cent of scheduled flights from Saudi airports were cancelled. At Riyadh’s King Khalid International Airport, the rate reached 86pc.

Direct Kathmandu-Dammam flights, widely used by Nepali workers, have also stopped. Nepal Airlines and Himalaya Airlines have cancelled 18 scheduled services since October 11. Nepal Airlines operates weekly and Himalaya twice a week; the latter has announced cancellations through November 4.

Around 400,000 Nepalis work in Saudi Arabia. The Department of Foreign Employment says about 7,000 people receive labour permits, including renewals, each month; 8,366 did so in the mid-September to mid-October period.

Nepali Embassy in Riyadh says the workers whose contracts have ended are under particular pressure. The embassy has asked employers to provide food and accommodation to the workers.

The embassy does not have official figures of the stranded Nepali workers. “More people are contacting us to ask where and from which airport they can travel home,” said labour counsellor Kabiraj Upreti. “We are facilitating whatever we can.”

Reuters reported on October 26 that 4,071 of 4,736 flights scheduled at Riyadh airport between October 8 and 25 had been cancelled. Cancellations reached 42pc in Dammam and 46.7pc in Abha. More than 7,800 flights, or 45pc of scheduled departures nationwide, were cancelled.

There are a total of 18 international airports in Saudi Arabia. Riyadh airport has partially reopened, but regular services have not returned. Some Saudi carrier flights have resumed, while foreign airlines have reduced or suspended Riyadh services. Jeddah and Dammam also face cancellations and rescheduling.

Madhendra Rai, an Ilam native working in Dammam, said repeated cancellation notices were causing mental stress. Airlines were not clearly explaining whether passengers could get refunds or transfer to another flight.

“When a flight is cancelled, they do not clearly explain the options. They tell us to take a voucher instead of a refund. Employers also say they will look for an alternative only after the cancellation is confirmed,” said Mahendra. “It is not just the ticket date that keeps changing; the day we can meet our families is also being pushed further away.”

Connecting flights through Air Arabia, flydubai and Indian carriers are also hard to find. “Even if we get a ticket, the one-way fare has reached Rs100,000. We have never seen tickets this expensive,” he said.

Dilip Baraili, another Nepali worker, said repeated flight cancellations had left ticket-holders in limbo. “The feelings of Nepalis who work hard abroad and wait to return home to celebrate festivals with their families must be understood,” he said.

Poor information is also adding to workers’ costs. Ganesh Rai’s October 25 Himalaya Airlines flight was cancelled, with rebooking arranged for October 30. That flight was cancelled, too, soon. The travel agency does not answer calls, he complained. Each fruitless trip to the airport costs him about Rs2,000.

Nepal Airlines said it had suspended flights for passenger safety. “This is not because of us,” said spokesperson Archana Khadka. “Services will resume as soon as the situation in Saudi Arabia becomes normal.”

The airline says passengers can change travel dates without charge or receive a full refund. Himalaya Airlines said its cancellations were also linked to aviation safety and that it could not guarantee a resumption date.

Umesh Pandey, working in Dammam, has waited 18 days to return to Nepal. He is considering travelling by road to Qatar or Bahrain but does not know the immigration procedures.

“If we cannot fly from Saudi Arabia, I want to travel by road to Qatar or Bahrain. But I do not know how to get the visa or whether border immigration will let us cross. We have never travelled this way,” said Umesh.

The problem is more serious for workers whose exit permits are near expiry. Hemanta Thapa, from Jhapa, works in Najran near the Yemeni border, where the regional airport is closed. His ticket has been cancelled and he fears he may miss Tihar. To catch a flight from Dammam, he must travel about 1,400 kilometres, a 17 to 18 hours road journey.

“For two years, I have been planning to go home for Tihar. I do not know when Dammam airport will reopen or when flights will operate,” he said.

Thapa had left his company after obtaining an exit permit, a process that took six months. If it expires before he can leave, he will have to apply again through the embassy. He says this could take another three months and he would have to bear the costs himself.

Workers have urged the government to arrange travel through neighbouring countries. “We are in trouble. The government should arrange flights home from Kuwait, Qatar or Bahrain,” said Shailesh Upadhyay. “Bahrain is the most suitable option.”

Balaram Thapa, president of the Non-Resident Nepali Association in Saudi Arabia, urged the government and airlines to arrange transport from Dammam to Bahrain. “It is close and we can reach it by bus or taxi. Some people are already travelling through Bahrain without being stopped at the border,” he said. “The government or airlines should arrange buses and direct flights to Nepal from there.”

The disruption comes amid wider security concerns. Houthi attacks had heightened fears among Nepalis, including workers in Dammam and Jizan. A report on October 22 said a Nepali and a Filipino were killed in a drone attack at the Shaybah oil field, while a Pakistani and an Indian worker were injured. The embassy has urged Nepalis to follow official alerts and verify flights before going to airports.

The foreign ministry says it is monitoring the situation. “The Nepali Embassy in Riyadh and the Consulate General in Jeddah are closely following the flights situation and facilities for Nepali citizens. They are in regular contact with Nepali citizens and communities,” said Lok Bahadur Paudel Chhetri, the ministry spokesperson.

“The government will take appropriate steps as necessary, keeping the convenience and safety of Nepali citizens in mind.”

It’s not only direct flights between Saudi Arabia and Nepal that have been cancelled. Connecting flights have also been affected. IndiGo has suspended services to Riyadh, Jeddah, Dammam and Medina until November 14. Air India and Air India Express have suspended flights to Riyadh and Dammam until November 7.

Similarly, Etihad Airways has cancelled some flights from Abu Dhabi to Riyadh, Dammam and Jeddah until November 5. Air Arabia has also cancelled some services to Riyadh, Dammam, Abha and Taif, but no resumption dates have been confirmed through publicly available sources.

Qatar Airways has suspended flights to Riyadh and Dammam and reduced the number of services to Jeddah. However, no new dates have been announced for the resumption of flights to Riyadh and Dammam following October 24.

article_html:
KATHMANDU: Rajesh Rai from Khotang was preparing to return home after three years in Saudi Arabia to celebrate Dashain with family. His employer had granted him a month’s leave and he had an exit-re-entry visa. He had booked an October 11 Air Arabia flight from Riyadh to Kathmandu via Sharjah.

But a day before departure, Houthi rebels attacked King Khalid International Airport. Thirteen people, according to Saudi authorities, were killed and more than 300 injured. The airport was shut.

After a friend told him that flights were operating from Jeddah, Rai travelled nearly 1,000 kilometres by bus for 13 hours, paying Rs7,000. But he remains in a friend’s room, unsure when he can fly home.

“I am neither in my company’s camp nor have I been able to reach home,” said Rai.

“Dashain has passed, Tihar is around the corner and my leave is about to end.”

Rai is among hundreds of Nepali workers whose plans to return home have been thrown into uncertainty. Between October 8 and 25, about 45 per cent of scheduled flights from Saudi airports were cancelled. At Riyadh’s King Khalid International Airport, the rate reached 86pc.

Direct Kathmandu-Dammam flights, widely used by Nepali workers, have also stopped. Nepal Airlines and Himalaya Airlines have cancelled 18 scheduled services since October 11. Nepal Airlines operates weekly and Himalaya twice a week; the latter has announced cancellations through November 4.

Around 400,000 Nepalis work in Saudi Arabia. The Department of Foreign Employment says about 7,000 people receive labour permits, including renewals, each month; 8,366 did so in the mid-September to mid-October period.

Nepali Embassy in Riyadh says the workers whose contracts have ended are under particular pressure. The embassy has asked employers to provide food and accommodation to the workers.

The embassy does not have official figures of the stranded Nepali workers. “More people are contacting us to ask where and from which airport they can travel home,” said labour counsellor Kabiraj Upreti. “We are facilitating whatever we can.”

Reuters reported on October 26 that 4,071 of 4,736 flights scheduled at Riyadh airport between October 8 and 25 had been cancelled. Cancellations reached 42pc in Dammam and 46.7pc in Abha. More than 7,800 flights, or 45pc of scheduled departures nationwide, were cancelled.

There are a total of 18 international airports in Saudi Arabia. Riyadh airport has partially reopened, but regular services have not returned. Some Saudi carrier flights have resumed, while foreign airlines have reduced or suspended Riyadh services. Jeddah and Dammam also face cancellations and rescheduling.

Madhendra Rai, an Ilam native working in Dammam, said repeated cancellation notices were causing mental stress. Airlines were not clearly explaining whether passengers could get refunds or transfer to another flight.

“When a flight is cancelled, they do not clearly explain the options. They tell us to take a voucher instead of a refund. Employers also say they will look for an alternative only after the cancellation is confirmed,” said Mahendra. “It is not just the ticket date that keeps changing; the day we can meet our families is also being pushed further away.”

Connecting flights through Air Arabia, flydubai and Indian carriers are also hard to find. “Even if we get a ticket, the one-way fare has reached Rs100,000. We have never seen tickets this expensive,” he said.

Dilip Baraili, another Nepali worker, said repeated flight cancellations had left ticket-holders in limbo. “The feelings of Nepalis who work hard abroad and wait to return home to celebrate festivals with their families must be understood,” he said.

Poor information is also adding to workers’ costs. Ganesh Rai’s October 25 Himalaya Airlines flight was cancelled, with rebooking arranged for October 30. That flight was cancelled, too, soon. The travel agency does not answer calls, he complained. Each fruitless trip to the airport costs him about Rs2,000.

Nepal Airlines said it had suspended flights for passenger safety. “This is not because of us,” said spokesperson Archana Khadka. “Services will resume as soon as the situation in Saudi Arabia becomes normal.”

The airline says passengers can change travel dates without charge or receive a full refund. Himalaya Airlines said its cancellations were also linked to aviation safety and that it could not guarantee a resumption date.

Umesh Pandey, working in Dammam, has waited 18 days to return to Nepal. He is considering travelling by road to Qatar or Bahrain but does not know the immigration procedures.

“If we cannot fly from Saudi Arabia, I want to travel by road to Qatar or Bahrain. But I do not know how to get the visa or whether border immigration will let us cross. We have never travelled this way,” said Umesh.

The problem is more serious for workers whose exit permits are near expiry. Hemanta Thapa, from Jhapa, works in Najran near the Yemeni border, where the regional airport is closed. His ticket has been cancelled and he fears he may miss Tihar. To catch a flight from Dammam, he must travel about 1,400 kilometres, a 17 to 18 hours road journey.

“For two years, I have been planning to go home for Tihar. I do not know when Dammam airport will reopen or when flights will operate,” he said.

Thapa had left his company after obtaining an exit permit, a process that took six months. If it expires before he can leave, he will have to apply again through the embassy. He says this could take another three months and he would have to bear the costs himself.

Workers have urged the government to arrange travel through neighbouring countries. “We are in trouble. The government should arrange flights home from Kuwait, Qatar or Bahrain,” said Shailesh Upadhyay. “Bahrain is the most suitable option.”

Balaram Thapa, president of the Non-Resident Nepali Association in Saudi Arabia, urged the government and airlines to arrange transport from Dammam to Bahrain. “It is close and we can reach it by bus or taxi. Some people are already travelling through Bahrain without being stopped at the border,” he said. “The government or airlines should arrange buses and direct flights to Nepal from there.”

The disruption comes amid wider security concerns. Houthi attacks had heightened fears among Nepalis, including workers in Dammam and Jizan. A report on October 22 said a Nepali and a Filipino were killed in a drone attack at the Shaybah oil field, while a Pakistani and an Indian worker were injured. The embassy has urged Nepalis to follow official alerts and verify flights before going to airports.

The foreign ministry says it is monitoring the situation. “The Nepali Embassy in Riyadh and the Consulate General in Jeddah are closely following the flights situation and facilities for Nepali citizens. They are in regular contact with Nepali citizens and communities,” said Lok Bahadur Paudel Chhetri, the ministry spokesperson.

“The government will take appropriate steps as necessary, keeping the convenience and safety of Nepali citizens in mind.”

It’s not only direct flights between Saudi Arabia and Nepal that have been cancelled. Connecting flights have also been affected. IndiGo has suspended services to Riyadh, Jeddah, Dammam and Medina until November 14. Air India and Air India Express have suspended flights to Riyadh and Dammam until November 7.

Similarly, Etihad Airways has cancelled some flights from Abu Dhabi to Riyadh, Dammam and Jeddah until November 5. Air Arabia has also cancelled some services to Riyadh, Dammam, Abha and Taif, but no resumption dates have been confirmed through publicly available sources.

Qatar Airways has suspended flights to Riyadh and Dammam and reduced the number of services to Jeddah. However, no new dates have been announced for the resumption of flights to Riyadh and Dammam following October 24.

Dilip Baraili, another Nepali worker, said repeated flight cancellations had left ticket-holders in limbo. “The feelings of Nepalis who work hard abroad and wait to return home to celebrate festivals with their families must be understood,” he said.

Poor information is also adding to workers’ costs. Ganesh Rai’s October 25 Himalaya Airlines flight was cancelled, with rebooking arranged for October 30. That flight was cancelled, too, soon. The travel agency does not answer calls, he complained. Each fruitless trip to the airport costs him about Rs2,000.

Nepal Airlines said it had suspended flights for passenger safety. “This is not because of us,” said spokesperson Archana Khadka. “Services will resume as soon as the situation in Saudi Arabia becomes normal.”

The airline says passengers can change travel dates without charge or receive a full refund. Himalaya Airlines said its cancellations were also linked to aviation safety and that it could not guarantee a resumption date.
Umesh Pandey, working in Dammam, has waited 18 days to return to Nepal. He is considering travelling by road to Qatar or Bahrain but does not know the immigration procedures.

“If we cannot fly from Saudi Arabia, I want to travel by road to Qatar or Bahrain. But I do not know how to get the visa or whether border immigration will let us cross. We have never travelled this way,” said Umesh.

The problem is more serious for workers whose exit permits are near expiry. Hemanta Thapa, from Jhapa, works in Najran near the Yemeni border, where the regional airport is closed. His ticket has been cancelled and he fears he may miss Tihar. To catch a flight from Dammam, he must travel about 1,400 kilometres, a 17 to 18 hours road journey.
“For two years, I have been planning to go home for Tihar. I do not know when Dammam airport will reopen or when flights will operate,” he said.

Thapa had left his company after obtaining an exit permit, a process that took six months. If it expires before he can leave, he will have to apply again through the embassy. He says this could take another three months and he would have to bear the costs himself.

Workers have urged the government to arrange travel through neighbouring countries. “We are in trouble. The government should arrange flights home from Kuwait, Qatar or Bahrain,” said Shailesh Upadhyay. “Bahrain is the most suitable option.”

Balaram Thapa, president of the Non-Resident Nepali Association in Saudi Arabia, urged the government and airlines to arrange transport from Dammam to Bahrain. “It is close and we can reach it by bus or taxi. Some people are already travelling through Bahrain without being stopped at the border,” he said. “The government or airlines should arrange buses and direct flights to Nepal from there.”

The disruption comes amid wider security concerns. Houthi attacks had heightened fears among Nepalis, including workers in Dammam and Jizan. A report on October 22 said a Nepali and a Filipino were killed in a drone attack at the Shaybah oil field, while a Pakistani and an Indian worker were injured. The embassy has urged Nepalis to follow official alerts and verify flights before going to airports.

The foreign ministry says it is monitoring the situation. “The Nepali Embassy in Riyadh and the Consulate General in Jeddah are closely following the flights situation and facilities for Nepali citizens. They are in regular contact with Nepali citizens and communities,” said Lok Bahadur Paudel Chhetri, the ministry spokesperson.
“The government will take appropriate steps as necessary, keeping the convenience and safety of Nepali citizens in mind.”

It’s not only direct flights between Saudi Arabia and Nepal that have been cancelled. Connecting flights have also been affected. IndiGo has suspended services to Riyadh, Jeddah, Dammam and Medina until November 14. Air India and Air India Express have suspended flights to Riyadh and Dammam until November 7.

Similarly, Etihad Airways has cancelled some flights from Abu Dhabi to Riyadh, Dammam and Jeddah until November 5. Air Arabia has also cancelled some services to Riyadh, Dammam, Abha and Taif, but no resumption dates have been confirmed through publicly available sources.

Qatar Airways has suspended flights to Riyadh and Dammam and reduced the number of services to Jeddah. However, no new dates have been announced for the resumption of flights to Riyadh and Dammam following October 24.

headline: Another Indian national injured in Riyadh airport attack dies
description: Another Indian national who was critically injured in the October 10 attack on Riyadh airport has died in an...
article_text:
Another Indian national who was critically injured in the October 10 attack on Riyadh airport has died in an intensive care unit (ICU), according to a statement.

The statement said the Indian authorities had remained in contact with the victim’s family and conveyed their condolences to his relatives and friends.

It added that all possible assistance would be extended to bring his remains back to India or arrange his funeral in Riyadh, depending on the family’s wishes.

headline: Numbers that tell the story of the Democrats' midterm blowout
description: Total turnout numbers were not in yet, but Americans cast more than 61.7 million votes even before election day.
author: AFP
article_text:
Democrats stormed back to power in Congress and governors’ mansions across America in Tuesday’s midterm elections, a stunning repudiation of Donald Trump’s political agenda.

These are the numbers that tell the tale of a historic night.

Record turnout

Total turnout numbers were not in yet, but Americans cast more than 61.7 million votes even before election day, according to the University of Florida’s Election Lab. That figure, a runaway record for early voting in US midterms, undoubtedly boosted Democrats, who traditionally cast their ballots early more often than Republican voters.

The numbers showed large turnout among African Americans, young people and other groups that typically support Democratic candidates, National Public Radio reported. The surge contributed to a wave election, with Democrats running the table on key races and seizing control of both chambers of Congress.

Record fundraising

Total spending for the 2026 midterms soared to a record $11.9 billion, substantially higher than the $8.9bn racked up in 2022, according to OpenSecrets, a non-partisan authority on spending in US politics.

Campaign fundraising and ad buys jumped in the 2026 races, driven by the outside spending of so-called political action committees. Such outside spending, led by Trump’s mega-billionaire ally Elon Musk, favoured Republicans by some $360m.

But Democratic candidates proved adept at raising their own funds. House and Senate candidates spent an unprecedented $3.7bn from their campaign war chests, with Democrats outspending Republicans by $800 million, according to OpenSecrets.

In Texas, Democratic Senate candidate James Talarico broke records by bringing in a staggering $145m, several times the $22m raised by his Republican rival Ken Paxton, who was forced to rely on outside groups to fund his campaign.

First wins in decades

Ninety-four years ago was the last time Kansas sent a Democrat to the US Senate. But on Tuesday night, Adam Hamilton unseated Republican incumbent Roger Marshall. Hamilton, the pastor of a Methodist megachurch who was registered as a Republican until recently, became the first Democrat to win a Senate race in the largely rural, conservative state since 1932.

Texas also went blue for the first time in decades, with Talarico scoring a massive upset to flip a Senate seat in the Lone Star State for the first time since 1988 — the year before Talarico was born.

South Carolina also defied history, ousting Senator Darline Graham — who had been appointed earlier this year to fill the seat of her late brother Lindsey Graham — in favour of Democrat Annie Andrews. No South Carolina Democrat had been elected to the Senate since 1998.

Young voters, Latinos turn away

Young men and Latino voters — two segments of the American electorate crucial to Trump — turned sharply away from the president and his Republican Party, exit polls showed.

Hispanic voters had helped bring Trump to power in 2016, and were instrumental in his victory in 2024, when they only narrowly went to Democrat Kamala Harris in the presidential election, 51 per cent to 48pc, according to Pew Research.

But in recent weeks, several Latino voters have expressed anger at Trump, saying they felt betrayed. It showed in NBC News exit polls on Tuesday, when Latino voters backed Democratic candidates by 62pc to 35pc over Republicans.

Young voters also soured on Trump. NBC News reported that its exit polls showed 18-29-year-olds, men and women, voted for Democrats by a 72pc to 25pc margin. That is a sharp shift from 2024, when young voters were split between Trump and Harris.

headline: Historic leadership firsts for minorities across US in midterm vote
description: The first Black female governor, the first openly gay male senator and the first female Native American governor all won groundbreaking elections in the vote that racked up resounding wins for Democrats.
author: AFP
article_text:
The US midterm vote ushered in a wave of historic leadership firsts across the country on Tuesday, electoral milestones on a night that saw voters issue a sharp rejection of President Donald Trump’s second term.

The first Black female governor, the first openly gay male senator and the first female Native American governor all won groundbreaking elections in the vote that racked up resounding wins for Democrats.

Bill Shiebler — chief strategy officer at the non-profit State Voices, a network of advocates for civic engagement and equity — told AFP the night was “a huge rebuke against hate and division.”

“We’re witnessing an electorate that increasingly sees itself in its leaders, and the leaders who come out of communities they now represent,” Shiebler said.

“I think that’s part of a multiracial democracy working as it’s intended, not just a novelty.”

In the southern state of Georgia, Democrat Keisha Lance Bottoms won the race for governor, making her the first Black woman elected to the top office in any US state.

A former Atlanta mayor, Bottoms defeated billionaire health care executive Rick Jackson, a win that returns the governor’s office to Democrats after more than two decades of Republican control.

Democratic Representative Chris Pappas, meanwhile, will become the first openly gay man to serve in the US Senate after winning in New Hampshire. He has served in the US House of Representatives since 2019.

“No one should be discriminated against because of who they are or who they love,” he said on his website.

In New Mexico, Democrat Deb Haaland became the first Native American woman elected governor, beating Republican Gregg Hull.

A member of the Laguna Pueblo tribe, she had served as the Secretary of the Interior under former president Joe Biden, the first Native American to serve as a US cabinet secretary.

‘Historic election’

And in Michigan, leftist Abdul El-Sayed won Michigan’s US Senate race over former Republican lawmaker Mike Rogers, US networks said, making him the first Muslim elected to the upper chamber of Congress.

The former medical administrator drew huge campaign crowds across Michigan with his promises to make healthcare free.

The sweeping midterm rebuke of Trump also saw a number of state-level electoral firsts, including the first Latina governor in Texas with Gina Hinojosa’s victory.

Looking ahead, if the current House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries wins the speakership as expected in the new Congress, he would become the first Black speaker of the House in US history.

“This was a historic election where people decided to believe in themselves and really lean into the hope about the promise of this country, rebuking an effort to snuff out people’s voices,” Shiebler said.

article_html:
The US midterm vote ushered in a wave of historic leadership firsts across the country on Tuesday, electoral milestones on a night that saw voters issue a sharp rejection of President Donald Trump’s second term.

The first Black female governor, the first openly gay male senator and the first female Native American governor all won groundbreaking elections in the vote that racked up resounding wins for Democrats.

Bill Shiebler — chief strategy officer at the non-profit State Voices, a network of advocates for civic engagement and equity — told AFP the night was “a huge rebuke against hate and division.”

“We’re witnessing an electorate that increasingly sees itself in its leaders, and the leaders who come out of communities they now represent,” Shiebler said.

“I think that’s part of a multiracial democracy working as it’s intended, not just a novelty.”

In the southern state of Georgia, Democrat Keisha Lance Bottoms won the race for governor, making her the first Black woman elected to the top office in any US state.

A former Atlanta mayor, Bottoms defeated billionaire health care executive Rick Jackson, a win that returns the governor’s office to Democrats after more than two decades of Republican control.

Democratic Representative Chris Pappas, meanwhile, will become the first openly gay man to serve in the US Senate after winning in New Hampshire. He has served in the US House of Representatives since 2019.

“No one should be discriminated against because of who they are or who they love,” he said on his website.

In New Mexico, Democrat Deb Haaland became the first Native American woman elected governor, beating Republican Gregg Hull.

A member of the Laguna Pueblo tribe, she had served as the Secretary of the Interior under former president Joe Biden, the first Native American to serve as a US cabinet secretary.

‘Historic election’

And in Michigan, leftist Abdul El-Sayed won Michigan’s US Senate race over former Republican lawmaker Mike Rogers, US networks said, making him the first Muslim elected to the upper chamber of Congress.

The former medical administrator drew huge campaign crowds across Michigan with his promises to make healthcare free.

The sweeping midterm rebuke of Trump also saw a number of state-level electoral firsts, including the first Latina governor in Texas with Gina Hinojosa’s victory.

Looking ahead, if the current House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries wins the speakership as expected in the new Congress, he would become the first Black speaker of the House in US history.

“This was a historic election where people decided to believe in themselves and really lean into the hope about the promise of this country, rebuking an effort to snuff out people’s voices,” Shiebler said.

headline: Israel election commission rejects Netanyahu charges of fraud
description: Central Elections Committee says it has conducted an audit of 9,069 polling stations following complaints and was confident that the announced results “accurately reflect the will of the voters”.
author: AFP
article_text:
Israeli electoral authorities on Wednesday rejected allegations promoted by Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu of fraud by Arab parties, who could hold the key to removing him from power after a divisive vote.

President Isaac Herzog will at noon (1000 GMT) officially receive the results of the October 27 election as he decides whether to give Netanyahu or his rival Gadi Eisenkot the first chance to form a government, with neither commanding enough votes alone.

The Central Elections Committee said it had conducted an audit of 9,069 polling stations following complaints and was confident that the announced results “accurately reflect the will of the voters”.

“All complaints submitted by political factions have been reviewed and there were no findings indicating harm to the integrity of the election,” it said in a statement.

Netanyahu has repeatedly alleged fraud by Arab-majority parties, pointing to the arrests of several people with envelopes of cash on election day and later claiming lawmakers received money from Qatar — allegations that have been levelled at his own aides in the past.

Late on Tuesday, Israeli Attorney General Gali Baharav-Miara said she would not question anyone without evidence after reports that the head of the domestic security service Shin Bet, a Netanyahu ally, had asked to interrogate Arab parties.

Netanyahu’s Likud party lashed out at her, saying that she was trying to “obstruct the investigation and to cover up this serious case of manipulation of the electoral process by foreign actors”.

Eisenkot, a former military chief trying to unite centrists and the centre-right and turn the page on Netanyahu’s long, polarising reign, accused Likud of attempting a “pogrom against democracy”.

He had earlier warned Netanyahu against launching a new war with his close ally US President Donald Trump against Iran, which could help the Israeli prime minister push for a unity government or to run out the clock until new elections.

No unity government

Yair Lapid, a former prime minister and key force in the opposition bloc, pointed to the midterm elections in the US in which Democrats resoundingly trounced Trump’s Republicans.

The Shin Bet “outbursts” paired with the US election results “eliminate any possibility of a unity government led by Netanyahu”.

Netanyahu, Israel’s longest-serving prime minister who has been in power on and off for nearly two decades, has called for a “broad national government” — with himself at the top.

Herzog’s statements have raised speculation that he could sound out leaders on a possible unity government, hoping to bring stability in a country sharply split after three years of war and over Netanyahu’s hard-right politics.

Herzog holds a largely ceremonial role as head of state, but carries the decisive vote on who will have the first chance to try to be prime minister — a process that could last weeks or even months and may end in failure and new elections.

After officially receiving the results, Herzog begins two days of consultations with parties, starting with the smaller ones.

Neither Netanyahu nor Eisenkot holds the 61 seats needed to secure a majority in the 120-member parliament.

Netanyahu’s bloc has an edge, with 53 seats as opposed to Eisenkot’s 48.

Eisenkot could reach the threshold if he were to ally with parties from the Arab minority, whose seat count surged to 19 on outrage against the actions and rhetoric of Netanyahu’s government.

But some in the opposition have baulked at relying on non-Jewish lawmakers’ votes.

‘Fresh thinking’

Herzog, a mild-mannered lawyer whose political career was in the defunct left-wing Labour Party but is now officially nonpartisan, has said he wants to encourage “fresh thinking” and avoid a new election.

Once Herzog tasks someone, they will have 28 days to form a government, with a potential 14-day extension.

If no one succeeds, Herzog will give the mandate to someone else. If that too fails, a majority of lawmakers could come together to nominate someone within 21 days — or else Israel heads to new elections.

It took Netanyahu, who at the time had a better showing by Likud, 58 days to form a government after the last election in November 2022.

Israel held five elections between 2019 and 2022 after repeated deadlocks.

Netanyahu faces corruption charges and the risk of jail if he loses power and, with it, immunity.

Yousef Jabareen, the head of the largest Arab-majority party in the next parliament, told AFP this week that the opposition needed to accept “political reality” and team up to remove Netanyahu.

Netanyahu has persistently warned Jewish Israelis that the opposition will work with Arab parties, which he accuses of backing Hamas.

headline: China says avoiding new hostilities in Mideast a 'top priority'
description: China says that avoiding a return to hostilities in the Middle East is a “top priority” in its diplomatic efforts...
article_text:
China says that avoiding a return to hostilities in the Middle East is a “top priority” in its diplomatic efforts with countries in the region.

Beijing has stepped up efforts in recent days to resolve the eight-month-long crisis after US President Donald Trump issued a fresh war threat against Iran over the weekend.

“The top priority is to avoid the resumption of hostilities in the Middle East that would bring disaster to the region’s people,” Beijing’s foreign ministry spokeswoman Mao Ning has told a news conference.

Beijing will “support Iran and the US in resolving disputes through negotiations, promote finding a political settlement to the Yemen issue, to help reach a proper and comprehensive solution for the opening of the Strait of Hormuz”, she has added.

headline: SSGC announces winter gas supply schedule for Sindh, Balochistan
description: Under the schedule, gas will be available from 6:30am to 9am, 12pm to 2:30pm and 6pm to 9pm.
author: Tahir Siddiqui
article_text:
KARACHI: The Sui Southern Gas Company (SSGC) on Wednesday announced the gas supply schedule for the winter season, under which three slots have been fixed for supply to domestic consumers, in line with federal government directives.

An SSGC spokesperson told Dawn that the schedule covers supply to domestic consumers in Sindh and Balochistan and comes into effect immediately.

Gas availability under new schedule:

6:30am-9am (Breakfast)
12pm-2:30pm (Lunch)
6pm-9pm (Dinner)

The SSGC shared the schedule on its website and social media platforms, saying that it was “prioritising domestic consumers by ensuring supply during meal times”.

For the past some years, SSGC’s consumers have not been getting round-the-clock gas supply.

On Tuesday, a severe gas crisis gripped Karachi. The situation was further complicated by multiple contradictory gas supply schedules attributed to SSGC that began circulating on social media from Monday. However, the utility had not issued any clear and consolidated statement until late Tuesday evening, adding to the confusion.

Gulf bourses advanced in early trade as investors weighed the fallout from the US midterms and waited to see how Washington would respond in its war with Iran, Reuters reports.

Democrats seized the Senate and the House, dealing a setback to President Donald Trump. Their wins in South Carolina, Texas and Ohio broke through long-held Republican territory.

Saudi Arabia’s benchmark index gained 1.7 per cent, lifted by a 6.7pc jump in Saudi Arabian Mining Company and a 1.4pc rise in Al Rajhi Bank.

headline: Top UN court to rule on Nov 19 on Myanmar's Rohingya genocide case
description: Judges at ICJ have for seven years been weighing accusations by The Gambia that Myanmar's brutal repression of the Rohingya breached the 1948 UN Genocide Convention.
author: AFP
article_text:
The top United Nations court will on November 19 deliver a landmark ruling on whether Myanmar’s crackdown against its mostly Muslim Rohingya minority constituted a genocide, officials said on Tuesday.

Judges at the International Court of Justice (ICJ) have for seven years been weighing accusations by The Gambia that Myanmar’s brutal repression of the Rohingya breached the 1948 UN Genocide Convention.

While the ICJ has no means of enforcing its decisions, a ruling that Myanmar committed genocide would heap more international pressure on its leader Min Aung Hlaing.

He commanded the military during the Rohingya crackdown before ousting the elected government of Aung San Suu Kyi in a 2021 coup.

This year he was installed as civilian president following deeply restricted elections and is waging a diplomatic campaign for legitimacy which may be complicated by the ruling.

The judgement may also be seen as justice for hundreds of thousands of Rohingya.

Legal experts are closely watching the decision by the ICJ, which rules in disputes between countries, for clues as to how the court might sway in the seminal genocide case brought by South Africa against Israel over its campaign in Gaza.

Myanmar has always denied carrying out a genocide against the Rohingya, arguing its actions targeted a military uprising from insurgents after a series of attacks left a dozen security personnel dead.

The crackdown by the Myanmar army and Buddhist militias forced hundreds of thousands of Rohingya to flee to neighbouring Bangladesh, bringing with them harrowing accounts of gang rape and mass executions.

More than one million Rohingya still live across the border in Bangladesh, in the world’s largest refugee settlement.

‘Collective conscience’

During hearings on the case in January, Gambian Justice Minister Dawda Jallow told the court the Rohingya had suffered “the most horrific violence and destruction one could imagine”.

“It is not about esoteric issues of international law. It is about real people, real stories and a real group of human beings,” said Jallow.

“The Rohingya of Myanmar. They have been targeted for destruction,” added the minister.

The Gambia has brought the case to the ICJ under the terms of the UN Genocide Convention, which allows any state to sound the alarm if it suspects genocide is being committed.

The alleged violations of the convention “are a stain on our collective conscience and it would be irresponsible to pretend that it is not our business”, Jallow said.

Myanmar retorted at the hearing that the allegations were “unsubstantiated”.

“Emotional language and blurry factual pictures are not a substitute for a rigorous presentation of facts,” said Ko Ko Hlaing, a minister in the president’s office.

In a previous hearing in 2019, de facto civilian leader Suu Kyi herself addressed the court, housed in the iconic Peace Palace in The Hague.

The Nobel peace laureate said the case risked reigniting the crisis that led to the Rohingya’s expulsion and said there was no “genocidal intent” behind the crackdown.

Suu Kyi, 81, will not be attending the verdict, however. She is under house arrest in the capital, Naypyidaw, authorities say, after being unseated in the 2021 military coup.

The ICJ has already made one ruling in this case, ordering Myanmar in 2020 to “take all measures within its power to prevent the commission of all acts” described by the Genocide Convention.

These acts included “killing members of the group” and “deliberately inflicting on the group conditions of life calculated to bring about its physical destruction in whole or in part”.

ICJ judges also threw out a challenge to its jurisdiction by Myanmar, ruling that it did have the power to decide on the genocide question.

The ICJ is not the only court looking into possible crimes against the Rohingya.

In 2024, the chief prosecutor of the International Criminal Court, also based in The Hague, asked judges for an arrest warrant for Min Aung Hlaing over alleged crimes against humanity.

A case is also underway in Argentina, under the principle of universal jurisdiction, the idea that some crimes are so heinous they can be heard in any court.
