article_html:
The top United Nations court will on November 19 deliver a landmark ruling on whether Myanmar’s crackdown against its mostly Muslim Rohingya minority constituted a genocide, officials said on Tuesday.

Judges at the International Court of Justice (ICJ) have for seven years been weighing accusations by The Gambia that Myanmar’s brutal repression of the Rohingya breached the 1948 UN Genocide Convention.

While the ICJ has no means of enforcing its decisions, a ruling that Myanmar committed genocide would heap more international pressure on its leader Min Aung Hlaing.

He commanded the military during the Rohingya crackdown before ousting the elected government of Aung San Suu Kyi in a 2021 coup.

This year he was installed as civilian president following deeply restricted elections and is waging a diplomatic campaign for legitimacy which may be complicated by the ruling.

The judgement may also be seen as justice for hundreds of thousands of Rohingya.

Legal experts are closely watching the decision by the ICJ, which rules in disputes between countries, for clues as to how the court might sway in the seminal genocide case brought by South Africa against Israel over its campaign in Gaza.

Myanmar has always denied carrying out a genocide against the Rohingya, arguing its actions targeted a military uprising from insurgents after a series of attacks left a dozen security personnel dead.

The crackdown by the Myanmar army and Buddhist militias forced hundreds of thousands of Rohingya to flee to neighbouring Bangladesh, bringing with them harrowing accounts of gang rape and mass executions.

More than one million Rohingya still live across the border in Bangladesh, in the world’s largest refugee settlement.

‘Collective conscience’

During hearings on the case in January, Gambian Justice Minister Dawda Jallow told the court the Rohingya had suffered “the most horrific violence and destruction one could imagine”.

“It is not about esoteric issues of international law. It is about real people, real stories and a real group of human beings,” said Jallow.

“The Rohingya of Myanmar. They have been targeted for destruction,” added the minister.

The Gambia has brought the case to the ICJ under the terms of the UN Genocide Convention, which allows any state to sound the alarm if it suspects genocide is being committed.

The alleged violations of the convention “are a stain on our collective conscience and it would be irresponsible to pretend that it is not our business”, Jallow said.

Myanmar retorted at the hearing that the allegations were “unsubstantiated”.

“Emotional language and blurry factual pictures are not a substitute for a rigorous presentation of facts,” said Ko Ko Hlaing, a minister in the president’s office.

In a previous hearing in 2019, de facto civilian leader Suu Kyi herself addressed the court, housed in the iconic Peace Palace in The Hague.

The Nobel peace laureate said the case risked reigniting the crisis that led to the Rohingya’s expulsion and said there was no “genocidal intent” behind the crackdown.

Suu Kyi, 81, will not be attending the verdict, however. She is under house arrest in the capital, Naypyidaw, authorities say, after being unseated in the 2021 military coup.

The ICJ has already made one ruling in this case, ordering Myanmar in 2020 to “take all measures within its power to prevent the commission of all acts” described by the Genocide Convention.

These acts included “killing members of the group” and “deliberately inflicting on the group conditions of life calculated to bring about its physical destruction in whole or in part”.

ICJ judges also threw out a challenge to its jurisdiction by Myanmar, ruling that it did have the power to decide on the genocide question.

The ICJ is not the only court looking into possible crimes against the Rohingya.

In 2024, the chief prosecutor of the International Criminal Court, also based in The Hague, asked judges for an arrest warrant for Min Aung Hlaing over alleged crimes against humanity.

A case is also underway in Argentina, under the principle of universal jurisdiction, the idea that some crimes are so heinous they can be heard in any court.

headline: Lebanon PM warns Hezbollah against joining another war
description: Lebanon’s prime minister warned against plunging the country into a new war if the Middle East conflict resumes, in...
article_text:
Lebanon’s prime minister warned against plunging the country into a new war if the Middle East conflict resumes, in an apparent message to Hezbollah, Reuters reports.

“Faced with the risks of renewed war in the region, I renew my warning of the dangers of dragging Lebanon into a new senseless adventure in service of outside interests,” Nawaf Salam said.

Iran-backed Hezbollah has twice pulled Lebanon into a war with Israel in as many years, most recently when it attacked Lebanon’s southern neighbour in support of Tehran in March.

“We do not accept the country again becoming a theatre for the conflict of others,” Salam added, saying Lebanon had “already paid a heavy price”.

headline: Schools in Sindh to remain closed on Nov 9 on account of Iqbal Day
description: According to the notification by the School Education and Literacy Department, all public and private schools shall remain closed.
author: News Desk
article_text:
The Sindh government announced on Wednesday that all public and private schools across the province would remain closed on Nov 9 (Monday) to mark the birth anniversary of Dr Allama Muhammad Iqbal, the national poet of Pakistan.

The Sindh Information Department posted a notification by the School Education and Literacy Department on the social media platform X.

“In pursuance of the decision taken in the meeting of Steering Committee on Education held on Feb 12, all public and private educational institutions under the administrative control of the School Education and Literacy Department, government of Sindh, shall remain closed on Nov 9 (Monday) on account of Allama Iqbal Day,” it said.

The notification was sent to the principal secretaries of the Sindh governor and chief minister, as well as other senior officials.

Born on November 9, 1877, in Sialkot, Iqbal was a distinguished poet, a scholar, a gifted philosopher and Pakistan’s ideological founder.

It was at the Allahabad session of the Muslim League in 1930 that Iqbal became the first politician to articulate the two-nation theory that ultimately led to the creation of Pakistan on August 14, 1947.

Iqbal Day was on the calendar of national public holidays for decades, but the interior ministry, through a circular issued on November 4, 2015, announced the cancellation of the day as an annual holiday without specifying a reason.

However, Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif’s government restored the holiday in 2022.

article_text:
Iran’s supreme leader Mojtaba Khamenei said that anyone expecting a shift in US policy was “seriously mistaken”, a day after US midterm elections dealt a blow to US President Donald Trump, AFP reports.

“Those who still harbour even the slightest hope that the behaviour of the hegemonic system might change through partisan or factional shifts, or who imagine that making concessions to the US can dissuade it from hostility towards the Iranian nation, are seriously mistaken,” he said in a written statement published on his website.

headline: Is cooking oil really the problem? Dr Yousuf Kamal Mirza explains 5 things every consumer should look for
description: The key is understanding which fats to choose and what to look for in the cooking oil we use every day.
author: ADVERTORIAL
article_text:
Cooking oil is an essential part of our everyday meals. From preparing breakfast to cooking family favorites, it plays an important role in our food and kitchens. Yet, many people tend to associate cooking oil with health concerns, often overlooking the fact that the type and quality of oil we consume also matter.

According to Yousuf Kamal Mirza, Senior Consultant Physician at Aga Khan University Hospital and Tabba Heart and Medilink Clinics, fats, just like carbohydrates, proteins and vitamins, are an integral part of our health. The key is understanding which fats to choose and what to look for in the cooking oil we use every day, he also emphasizes that choosing a cooking oil should go beyond taste, price and everyday convenience. Consumers should pay attention to its nutritional composition, quality and performance during cooking.

Dr Mirza highlights five important considerations when selecting cooking oil:

Zero Cholesterol and Unsaturated Fats: Choose cooking oils that are cholesterol-free and contain unsaturated fats, including monounsaturated and polyunsaturated fats, as important nutritional attributes to consider when making informed choices for everyday cooking and supports heart health“
Omega 3 and Omega 6: Essential fatty acids that support normal bodily functions.
Vitamins A, D and E: Important fat-soluble vitamins that contribute to various bodily functions.
Less Oil Absorption: An important consideration for the amount of oil absorbed by food during cooking.
High Quality Refining: An essential factor in the quality of cooking oil.

Iran’s supreme leader Ayatollah Mojtaba Khamenei warned that the Middle East war would become even wider if the United States resumed its attacks on the Islamic republic, AFP reports.

headline: Iran threatens to target ‘enemy leaders’ if its commanders are attacked, IRGC adviser says
description: An adviser to the commander-in-chief of Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) warns that Tehran will...
article_text:
An adviser to the commander-in-chief of Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) warns that Tehran will target “enemy leaders” if Iranian commanders and leaders are attacked in any renewed conflict, Anadolu reports.

“If they target our commanders and leaders this time, they should expect their own commanders and leaders to be killed,” Mohammad Moghadamfar says, according to Iran’s Fars News Agency.

He further warns that Iran will adopt new methods in confronting any renewed war, warning that its response will no longer be reciprocal or proportional.

“Our responses will no longer be reciprocal or proportional. We will go beyond the point of attack and set their assets ablaze, regardless of time or place,” he stresses.

headline: Pakistan, UK express concern at threat posed by terrorist groups operating in and from Afghanistan: FO
description: Underscore the “urgent need for a stable, secure Afghanistan as a cornerstone for lasting peace and prosperity across the region”.
author: News Desk
article_text:
Pakistan and the United Kingdom on Wednesday expressed concerns over the ongoing threat from terrorist groups operating in and from Afghanistan, the Foreign Office said.

According to a statement by the FO, the two countries held their annual bilateral dialogue on counter-terrorism in Islamabad, in which they reviewed ongoing bilateral and multilateral counter-terrorism cooperation and reaffirmed their shared commitment to combatting terrorism in all its forms.

“The two sides discussed in detail the evolving regional and global security environment and exchanged views on the threats posed by terrorist entities, including transnational terrorist networks,” it said.

“Both sides expressed concerns over the continuing threat posed by terrorist groups, including the Tehreek-i-Taliban Pakistan (TTP), operating in and from Afghanistan,” the FO said, adding that they underscored the “urgent need for a stable, secure Afghanistan as a cornerstone for lasting peace and prosperity across the region”.

The UK delegation also expressed condolences over the loss of innocent lives in terrorist attacks in Pakistan and reiterated that it stood with the country in the fight against terrorism, the statement added.

Another focus of the dialogue was the exchange of best practices and the exploration of new avenues for partnership to counter new trends in terrorism, including campaigns of misinformation and disinformation, exploitation of social media platforms and emerging technologies, it said.

“Both sides acknowledged Pakistan’s contributions to regional stability and security,” the FO said, adding that they agreed to strengthen institutional linkages and maintain regular engagement to advance shared counter-terrorism objectives.

According to the statement, the delegations agreed to hold the next round of the dialogue in London in 2027, on mutually agreed dates.

Earlier this year, the two countries agreed to enhance cooperation in counterterrorism, combating illegal migration and human smuggling, institutional collaboration and police training.

Pakistan and the European Union (EU) have also agreed to strengthen cooperation at multilateral forums, including the United Nations.

Ties between Pakistan and Afghanistan have been strained in the past few years as Islamabad continues to voice its concern over cross-border terrorism.

Islamabad has repeatedly urged the Taliban administration in Kabul to dismantle terrorist sanctuaries on Afghan soil, particularly those linked to the banned TTP that are used for attacks in Pakistan. Officials say those appeals have gone unheeded.

article_html:
Pakistan and the United Kingdom on Wednesday expressed concerns over the ongoing threat from terrorist groups operating in and from Afghanistan, the Foreign Office said.

According to a statement by the FO, the two countries held their annual bilateral dialogue on counter-terrorism in Islamabad, in which they reviewed ongoing bilateral and multilateral counter-terrorism cooperation and reaffirmed their shared commitment to combatting terrorism in all its forms.

“The two sides discussed in detail the evolving regional and global security environment and exchanged views on the threats posed by terrorist entities, including transnational terrorist networks,” it said.

“Both sides expressed concerns over the continuing threat posed by terrorist groups, including the Tehreek-i-Taliban Pakistan (TTP), operating in and from Afghanistan,” the FO said, adding that they underscored the “urgent need for a stable, secure Afghanistan as a cornerstone for lasting peace and prosperity across the region”.

The UK delegation also expressed condolences over the loss of innocent lives in terrorist attacks in Pakistan and reiterated that it stood with the country in the fight against terrorism, the statement added.

Another focus of the dialogue was the exchange of best practices and the exploration of new avenues for partnership to counter new trends in terrorism, including campaigns of misinformation and disinformation, exploitation of social media platforms and emerging technologies, it said.

“Both sides acknowledged Pakistan’s contributions to regional stability and security,” the FO said, adding that they agreed to strengthen institutional linkages and maintain regular engagement to advance shared counter-terrorism objectives.

According to the statement, the delegations agreed to hold the next round of the dialogue in London in 2027, on mutually agreed dates.

Earlier this year, the two countries agreed to enhance cooperation in counterterrorism, combating illegal migration and human smuggling, institutional collaboration and police training.

Pakistan and the European Union (EU) have also agreed to strengthen cooperation at multilateral forums, including the United Nations.

Ties between Pakistan and Afghanistan have been strained in the past few years as Islamabad continues to voice its concern over cross-border terrorism.

Islamabad has repeatedly urged the Taliban administration in Kabul to dismantle terrorist sanctuaries on Afghan soil, particularly those linked to the banned TTP that are used for attacks in Pakistan. Officials say those appeals have gone unheeded.

headline: Trump hand-picked Senate candidates. Republicans paid the price
description: “Trump spent the year telling voters what was important to him, not to them,” says Republican strategist Doug Heye.
author: Reuters
article_text:
US President Donald Trump asked voters to pretend he was on the ballot in the midterm elections and handpicked Republican candidates in some of the country’s most consequential Senate races. By Tuesday night, voters had rejected them.

Trump-backed candidates in South Carolina, North Carolina and Texas all lost, while the president’s preferred pick trailed in early results in Michigan. The defeats handed Democrats control of the chamber and exposed the limits of Trump’s political power.

Trump has spent more than a decade reshaping the Republican Party around his ‘Make America Great Again’ (MAGA) movement, dictating primary matchups and pushing aside conservative figures he felt were insufficiently loyal or not aligned with his vision.

Trump repeatedly favoured loyalists and ideological allies over more established Republicans with stronger statewide networks and proven electoral track records, betting that his endorsement could overcome their political liabilities.

Tuesday’s results revealed he was unable to persuade the broader electorate to back his choices.

One of the most stunning repudiations came in South Carolina, which had not elected a Democratic senator since 1998 and which Trump won by 18 percentage points in 2024. Trump backed Darline Graham, the sister of late Republican Senator Lindsey Graham. But Democrat Annie Andrews won the seat in a stunning upset.

In North Carolina, Trump endorsed former national Republican campaign official Michael Whatley, who lost in a rout to former Democratic Governor Roy Cooper.

In Texas, Trump intervened in a messy Republican primary election to promote scandal-plagued Attorney General Ken Paxton over Senator John Cornyn, a Trump ally who some in the party considered a safer pick in the general election. Democrat James Talarico glided to a victory on Tuesday night, delivering Democrats a seat the party had not won since 1988.

Former US Representative Mike Rogers, Trump’s choice in Michigan, trailed Democrat Abdul El-Sayed in an uncalled race. El-Sayed would be the first Muslim to serve in the Senate.

The losses came as Trump’s popularity was lower heading into Tuesday’s vote than in the aftermath of the January 6, 2021, attack on the US Capitol, according to Reuters/Ipsos polls. That helped fuel concerns among Republicans that the president had become a drag on the party he remade around himself.

This is a “Trump Quake”, said Doug Heye, a veteran Republican strategist, pointing to voter frustration over high prices caused by tariffs and the war in Iran.

“Trump spent the year telling voters what was important to him, not to them.”

Trump struck a defiant tone as election returns arrived.

“I wasn’t on the ballot, and if I was, we would have won in a landslide!” Trump wrote in a Tuesday night social media post.

One White House official, speaking on condition of anonymity, said Trump did a better job promoting many of the candidates on the ballot than the candidates did themselves.

A senior White House official, also speaking anonymously, told Reuters the administration had polling data as far back as six weeks ago showing Republicans would lose both the House of Representatives and Senate, and Trump embarked on a month-long nationwide campaign to try to salvage Republicans’ prospects.

‘Gave that seat away’

Some independent analysts said the Senate losses bore Trump’s fingerprints specifically.

Thomas Kahn, a professor at American University, said the president’s intervention in the Texas Republican primary had cost his party a safe seat, arguing that a nomination for Senator John Cornyn “would have been a slam dunk for Republicans to win.”

North Carolina, Kahn said, was another clear case. The Republican incumbent senator, Thom Tillis, said he would not seek re-election last year after a public split with Trump, who threatened to back a primary challenger against him after Tillis baulked at Medicaid cuts in the president’s tax-and-spending bill.

“He essentially gave that seat away to Democrats,” Kahn said. “Roy Cooper would not have run if Thom Tillis had run for re-election.” Former North Carolina Governor Pat McCrory, a Republican, said Trump’s interventions in his party’s primaries had divided Republicans in state after state.

In South Carolina, McCrory said, the president went against two local congressmen, a fight that “really divided the party”, an example, in his telling, of a president spending his political capital against his own side.

McCrory’s sharpest criticism was aimed at Trump’s connection with the voters who built his coalition.

“I think President Trump’s greatest strength was that he had a common touch with the working-class people,” McCrory said. “He lost that skill. He better regain that skill for the good of the country.”

“Trump spent the year telling voters what was important to him, not to them.”
Trump struck a defiant tone as election returns arrived.
“I wasn’t on the ballot, and if I was, we would have won in a landslide!” Trump wrote in a Tuesday night social media post.
One White House official, speaking on condition of anonymity, said Trump did a better job promoting many of the candidates on the ballot than the candidates did themselves.

A senior White House official, also speaking anonymously, told Reuters the administration had polling data as far back as six weeks ago showing Republicans would lose both the House of Representatives and Senate, and Trump embarked on a month-long nationwide campaign to try to salvage Republicans’ prospects.
‘Gave that seat away’
Some independent analysts said the Senate losses bore Trump’s fingerprints specifically.

Thomas Kahn, a professor at American University, said the president’s intervention in the Texas Republican primary had cost his party a safe seat, arguing that a nomination for Senator John Cornyn “would have been a slam dunk for Republicans to win.”

North Carolina, Kahn said, was another clear case. The Republican incumbent senator, Thom Tillis, said he would not seek re-election last year after a public split with Trump, who threatened to back a primary challenger against him after Tillis baulked at Medicaid cuts in the president’s tax-and-spending bill.

“He essentially gave that seat away to Democrats,” Kahn said. “Roy Cooper would not have run if Thom Tillis had run for re-election.” Former North Carolina Governor Pat McCrory, a Republican, said Trump’s interventions in his party’s primaries had divided Republicans in state after state.

In South Carolina, McCrory said, the president went against two local congressmen, a fight that “really divided the party”, an example, in his telling, of a president spending his political capital against his own side.
McCrory’s sharpest criticism was aimed at Trump’s connection with the voters who built his coalition.

“I think President Trump’s greatest strength was that he had a common touch with the working-class people,” McCrory said. “He lost that skill. He better regain that skill for the good of the country.”

headline: Oil falls on Iran war uncertainty, US Democrats' midterm sweep
description: Oil prices fell on Wednesday in volatile trading as investors awaited Washington’s next move in the US-Israeli war...
article_text:
Oil prices fell on Wednesday in volatile trading as investors awaited Washington’s next move in the US-Israeli war with Iran, after the Democrats captured control of Congress from President Donald Trump’s Republicans in the midterm elections, Reuters reports.

Brent futures were down $1.49, or 1.44 per cent, to $102.11 a barrel at 1155 GMT. US West Texas Intermediate crude futures were down 89 cents, or 0.93pc, to $95.20. Both had risen $1 earlier.

Brent in the previous session settled at its lowest level in nearly four weeks as traders weighed talks to end the wars in Ukraine and Iran.

headline: Federal cabinet ratifies defence agreement with Kuwait
description: According to the PMO, the cabinet also approved the transfer of powers from the KP chief minister to the governor and the design of new currency notes.
author: News Desk
article_text:
The federal cabinet on Wednesday ratified the defence cooperation agreement between Pakistan and Kuwait, according to a handout by the Prime Minister’s Office (PMO).

“The federal cabinet ratified a defence cooperation agreement between Pakistan and Kuwait. This agreement, which aims to foster cooperation in the defence sector between the two brotherly nations, was concluded on June 11, 2023. The Kuwaiti government had ratified the agreement on July 19,” the handout said.

In 2023, Pakistan and Kuwait signed a defence pact to further strengthen defe­nce cooperation and institutional linkages between the armed forces of the two countries.

The statement also said that the cabinet approved the transfer of powers delegated to the Khyber Pakhtunkhwa chief minister to the province’s governor. The Centre declared an emergency and governor’s rule in the province on Oct 11.

It said the powers included “the conduct of day-to-day affairs during the period of emergency in the province, to facilitate the smooth handling of administrative matters in KP and further improve governance”.

“The KP governor will submit a review report to the federal government every month regarding the exercise of all such powers,” the statement said.

It stated that the federal cabinet welcomed the decision and expressed the hope that the KP Advisory Council, under the leadership of the Governor Faisal Karim Kundi, would make full efforts for the welfare and prosperity of the people of the province and for establishing peace and security.

Moreover, the federal cabinet, on the recommendation of the Ministry of Finance, approved the design of new currency notes, the statement added.

“The cabinet was given a detailed briefing on the new currency notes. The briefing stated that proposals were solicited from artists and designers across the country for the design of the new currency notes and a cabinet committee established by the prime minister conducted detailed consultations on it with all stakeholders,” the handout said.

According to the statement, the meeting was informed that, along with enhancing security features to prevent counterfeit notes, modern materials would be used, which would also extend the lifespan of the notes.

The federal cabinet also approved the introduction of a Rs10 coin in place of the Rs10 banknote, the PMO statement said.

‘Pakistan continuing efforts for peace in Middle East’

Addressing the federal cabinet during televised remarks, Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif noted that global oil prices had “skyrocketed” due to the instability in the region.

“Pakistan is playing its role as before in restoring peace in the region,” he said, recalling Pakistan’s recent engagements with Tehran and other regional actors in the matter, as well as engagements under the Makkah Joint Defence Agreement between Pakistan, Saudi Arabia and Turkiye.

Last month, Chief of Defence Forces and Chief of Army Staff Field Marshal Asim Munir, accompanied by Interior Minister Mohsin Naqvi, visited Iran as part of Pakistan’s efforts to mediate between Washington and Tehran.

In another meeting in October, held under the Makkah Joint Defence Agreement, CDF Munir, the Saudi defence minister, and the Turkish spymaster met top Iranian officials in Tehran. Last week, the military’s spokesman said Pakistan remained “cautiously optimistic” about its mediation between the US and Iran.

On Tuesday, PM Shehbaz also recalled that the government had planned to hike fuel prices by Rs15 on Friday.

“Petroleum Minister Ali Pervaiz Malik [..] talked to the refineries to bear the burden in their windfall profits. We will not let a common man bear this burden,” he added.

Speaking about the fuel subsidy scheme, launched in September, the premier said it would run till the end of December.

“Rs28 billion has been spent so far,” he said, adding that the scheme was running “successfully and transparently” and that the Intelligence Bureau (IB) continued to monitor it.

On liquefied petroleum gas (LPG), the prime minister said that the “era of mafiaa” was over and it was now being arranged transparently.

“Now when LPG is imported, competition will be promoted and it will be auctioned in lots. The government will take the profits and subsidise it for the common man,” he said.

He also stressed that the federal government was holding meetings “day and night” to meet LPG, liquefied natural gas (LNG), petrol and gas requirements ahead of winter despite challenges arising from the closure of maritime routes.

LPG supply has been disrupted in the country due to the closure of Iranian border crossings, resulting in gas cylinders being sold at twice the official rate in the open market.

PM Shehbaz also said that the federal government had finalised a proposed Rs160bn package for Khyber Pakhtunkhwa.

“Security is our number one, two and three priority in KP,” the premier remarked. He further noted that counterterrorism efforts continued in the region.

With the efforts of law enforcement agencies, the new government in KP and the support of the federal government, we will crush terrorism,” he said.

In another meeting in October, held under the Makkah Joint Defence Agreement, CDF Munir, the Saudi defence minister, and the Turkish spymaster met top Iranian officials in Tehran. Last week, the military’s spokesman said Pakistan remained “cautiously optimistic” about its mediation between the US and Iran.
On Tuesday, PM Shehbaz also recalled that the government had planned to hike fuel prices by Rs15 on Friday.
“Petroleum Minister Ali Pervaiz Malik [..] talked to the refineries to bear the burden in their windfall profits. We will not let a common man bear this burden,” he added.
Speaking about the fuel subsidy scheme, launched in September, the premier said it would run till the end of December.
“Rs28 billion has been spent so far,” he said, adding that the scheme was running “successfully and transparently” and that the Intelligence Bureau (IB) continued to monitor it.
On liquefied petroleum gas (LPG), the prime minister said that the “era of mafiaa” was over and it was now being arranged transparently.
“Now when LPG is imported, competition will be promoted and it will be auctioned in lots. The government will take the profits and subsidise it for the common man,” he said.

He also stressed that the federal government was holding meetings “day and night” to meet LPG, liquefied natural gas (LNG), petrol and gas requirements ahead of winter despite challenges arising from the closure of maritime routes.
LPG supply has been disrupted in the country due to the closure of Iranian border crossings, resulting in gas cylinders being sold at twice the official rate in the open market.
PM Shehbaz also said that the federal government had finalised a proposed Rs160bn package for Khyber Pakhtunkhwa.
“Security is our number one, two and three priority in KP,” the premier remarked. He further noted that counterterrorism efforts continued in the region.
With the efforts of law enforcement agencies, the new government in KP and the support of the federal government, we will crush terrorism,” he said.

headline: 'Clear message' by Americans: US politicians react to Democratic win in US midterms
description: Republican John Thune says cannot let Democrats' fringe positions "become mainstream".
author: News Desk
article_text:
In a sweeping midterm rout, Democrats won control of the US Congress, with a series of upsets delivering a major rebuke to President Donald Trump and his Republican Party.

The victory handed Democrats both the House of Representatives and Senate, giving them power to block Trump’s agenda and investigate alleged corruption for the last two years of his presidency.

Many politicians, Democrats and Republicans alike, reacted as news of America’s choice broke, with the former rejoicing countrywide.

Former US president Bill Clinton said Democrats will lower costs, protect healthcare, end senseless wars, while also stopping tariffs that make life more expensive.

“You deserve a government that works as hard for you as you do for your family,” Clinton posted on X. “It’s high time we put people first again!”

Former US president Barack Obama said the results were a “clear message” from the Americans.

“They want a politics that brings people together rather than divides them, and leaders who offer concrete solutions to the challenges they face,” Obama said on X.

“These results were only possible because outstanding candidates stepped forward in every region of the country,” he added.

“While this administration has another two years in office, our job now is to roll up our sleeves, make changes wherever we have the power to do so, prevent further damage, and lay the groundwork for the future,” Obama further asserted.

President Trump, meanwhile, in comments to Fox News, said, “Congratulations to the Democrats — they did a good job. They’ve been looking for this one for 11 years and they finally got it.”

He added, “I don’t view it as a hit on me.”

US Senator Bernie Sanders called the news “great” on X.

“At a time of massive income and wealth inequality, we must do more. We must aggressively fight for working families. No more excuses,” he wrote.

Former US vice president Kamala Harris reacted to the news with a video of herself saying, “Hallelujah!”

Democratic Representative Robert Garcia, now expected to lead the powerful House Oversight Committee, in a post on X warned Republicans on social media: “LAWYER UP.”

House Democratic leader Hakeem Jeffries declared Trump’s MAGA movement “on the run from sea to shining sea”. Jeffries could become the first Black speaker of the House when the new Congress convenes in January.

Former secretary of transportation Pete Buttigieg, in the wake of a number of Republican strongholds flipping blue, said, “Tonight proves it: there is no such thing as a permanently red seat.”

Senate Majority Leader John Thune, in a post on X, vowed: “As we head into 2027, Senate Republicans will not stand idly by as the far-left, socialist wing of the Democratic Party attempts to unwind everything we’ve done.”

He expressed gratitude that Trump was still in the White House, hoping that the Republicans will “work with him to stop the worst impulses of Democrat extremism. We cannot let their fringe positions become the mainstream”.

Florida Governor Ron DeSantis pointed out that it was “unlikely” Republicans would recapture Congress in 2028, looking at the Senate map and given the “massive” margin in the House.

“Might not have a shot at Senate control until 2032,” he added.

CNN cited DeSantis as saying that Republicans underemphasised the impact of high gas prices due to the Iran war, although he did not name Trump specifically.

“Listen, we’ve just got to be honest. Gas is higher. It hurts people, working-class people, and it’s higher because of the Iran conflict […] If you can’t admit that to voters, then you’re gaslighting them,” DeSantis said on Stephen A. Smith’s podcast “Straight Shooter” on Monday, according to CNN.

Former US Congresswoman Marjorie Taylor Greene, reacting to the development, said it was a “total referendum” for Trump, accusing the US president of “covering up the Epstein files, protecting rapists and paedophiles” and starting the US-Iran war.

She said Trump “killed a school full of kids, put his rich elite donors before the struggling Americans who put him in office, made life unaffordable with his tariffs, and caused gas and diesel prices to skyrocket while he played the market and sold crypto.”

“And Republicans stood behind him silently clapping like trained baby seals,” she said.

“And tonight they sent him a clear message,” she added, warning that Republicans “need to learn the lesson and drastically change course”.

“And I’m not sure if they’re capable of that.”

headline: Baqaei says American people have sent a 'clear message', warns of consequences of 'grave miscalculation' by US
description: “Pride comes before a fall,” Iran’s foreign ministry spokesperson Esmaeil Baqaei says in a post on X, referring to...
article_text:
“Pride comes before a fall,” Iran’s foreign ministry spokesperson Esmaeil Baqaei says in a post on X, referring to the US.

“You dragged your country into an unlawful and atrocious war against Iran. Your calculations failed, your assumptions collapsed, and your strategic misjudgments became painfully evident — all because you fundamentally misunderstood Iran,” he says.

“The American people have now sent you a clear message.”

He warns that if the US persists with the war, “the consequences of this grave miscalculation will extend far beyond what you have already witnessed”.

“Attacking Iran does not bring victory. It only results in defeat,” the spokesperson adds. “Iran is not a nation that can be understood through arrogance, intimidated through threats, or brought to its knees through aggression.”

headline: Iran supreme leader says those expecting US policy shift 'seriously mistaken'
description: “Should such aggressions be repeated, the war's scope will become much wider,” Ayatollah Mojtaba Khamenei warns.
author: AFP
article_text:
Iran’s supreme leader Ayatollah Mojtaba Khamenei said on Wednesday that anyone expecting a shift in US policy was “seriously mistaken”, hours after midterm elections dealt a blow to President Donald Trump.

“Those who still harbour even the slightest hope that the behaviour of the hegemonic system might change through partisan or factional shifts, or who imagine that making concessions to the United States can dissuade it from hostility towards the Iranian nation, are seriously mistaken,” Khamenei said in a written statement published on his website.

Democrats seized control of the US Congress in Tuesday’s midterms, reflecting anger over living costs, tariffs and the US war against Iran, which has sent fuel prices soaring.

Khamenei’s remarks come with diplomatic efforts underway to avert renewed fighting in the war, which broke out on February 28. US and Israeli leaders have in recent days threatened to resume attacks against Iran.

“Should such aggressions be repeated, the war’s scope will become much wider,” said Khamenei, who has yet to appear in public since he took power in March.

Earlier, Iran’s chief negotiator in talks with the US, Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf, said Americans had voted against war.

“Conscience or the cost of living, Americans said NO TO WAR, and we endorse this message,” he posted on X.

“If the US govt betrays their public will to serve international paymasters and blackmailers, it will learn our NO comes with a Nightmare,” Ghalibaf said.

Iran’s judiciary chief Gholamhossein Mohseni Ejei also hailed the election results, saying Trump had been “defeated both militarily and politically”.

“We will certainly inflict further defeats on him,” he added.

headline: 'We did it!': Democrat El-Sayed hails US Senate win, becomes first Muslim elected to upper chamber of Congress
description: Addressing US Vice President Vance, El-Sayed says in his victory speech: “You're constitutionally obligated to swear me in in January".
author: AFP, News Desk
article_text:
Democrat Abdul El-Sayed won Michigan’s US Senate race over former Republican lawmaker Mike Rogers, US networks said early on Wednesday, making him the first Muslim elected to the upper chamber of Congress.

“Michigan, we did it!” El-Sayed said in a speech attended by hundreds of supporters who screamed and hugged each other at his election headquarters in Detroit.

“I am so proud and honored to stand here as your senator-elect from the great state of Michigan.”

El-Sayed won despite a last-minute curve ball in his campaign when congresswoman Haley Stevens, who lost the Democratic primary to El-Sayed, came out in support of Rogers at the 11th hour.

The Michigan medical administrator rallied voters on leftist campaign promises, including universal health care, to win a key US Senate seat for Democrats, taking over from the retiring Gary Peters.

El-Sayed held a nearly six-point lead on Rogers when networks called the race.

Party-goer entrepreneur Trunetta Roach, 75, who attended El-Sayed’s victory party in downtown Detroit wearing US flag-design diamante high-heels, said: “We are sick and tired of being sick and tired. And I’m so proud of all the work. It was boots on the ground. We were always out, but we were never outworked.”

“I’m feeling elated. The kids are all right. I was concerned about them.

They didn’t seem very engaged, but I was wrong. They showed up.”

‘Swear me in’

Republicans ran a scorched-earth campaign to paint Democrats as communists and branded El-Sayed a terrorist who would endanger Americans.

But the straight-talking 42-year-old El-Sayed pledged to help cash-strapped voters navigate America’s fractured, for-profit health care system.

“You deserve to be able to see a doctor without getting a huge bill,” he told Michiganders on the eve of the vote, vowing to upend America’s divisive multi-billion-dollar for-profit medical system.

During the race, El-Sayed drew huge campaign crowds across the state, even in deeply conservative Republican areas.

El-Sayed also vowed to get “money out of politics” and address the harsh economic woes that have voters yearning for a political newcomer to shake up the status quo.

The victory made El-Sayed the first Democratic doctor in the Senate since 1969.

“Everybody in politics is so trash. So to see ethical Muslims be at the forefront representing us and showing everybody what we’re actually about … it means everything,” said micro-influencer Maryam Bozai, 28.

At the victory party, crowds gathered around TVs tuned to left-leaning cable news channel MS NOW, cheering jubilantly each time the Democrat’s trademark blue flashed on screen to announce another race won by the party.

“Tsunami! Tsunami!” chanted Ondine Fortune, 64, a Democratic Party media planner.

El-Sayed supporters rubbed shoulders with left-leaning influencers and union activists, a group that lent El-Sayed their formidable campaign infrastructure to reach Michigan’s large organised labour community.

Eboni Taylor, a vice-president at Higher Heights which promotes Black women seeking office, said El-Sayed had “gone places where I just would not expect to see him.”

“What’s most remarkable is that he’s showing up in places that are not the usual prescription for the Democratic Party. He’s going wherever the people want him to be,” Taylor said between social media livestreams and celebratory dancing.

El-Sayed faced Islamophobic attacks and mockery for his Arabic name from US President Donald Trump and Vice President JD Vance. But El-Sayed may yet have the last laugh.

Addressing the vice president, El-Sayed said in his victory speech, “you’re constitutionally obligated to swear me in in January”.

Dr Arif Alvi congratulates El-Sayed

Pakistan’s former president Dr Arif Alvi congratulated El-Sayed on his victory in a post on X and said it “resonates far beyond one election”.

“It is a reminder that democracy matters: that the people’s mandate is sacred, that every vote counts, and that the will of the people cannot be wished away, manipulated or denied with guns,” he said, wishing El-Sayed success in his role.

Alvi added that “being Muslim should never make anyone a target of hatred, prejudice or intimidation. No one should have to face the vile excesses of Islamophobia.”

He noted that the “people’s voice will prevail”, expressing his hope that the lesson would reach beyond US shores.

“I am so proud and honored to stand here as your senator-elect from the great state of Michigan.”

El-Sayed won despite a last-minute curve ball in his campaign when congresswoman Haley Stevens, who lost the Democratic primary to El-Sayed, came out in support of Rogers at the 11th hour.

Party-goer entrepreneur Trunetta Roach, 75, who attended El-Sayed’s victory party in downtown Detroit wearing US flag-design diamante high-heels, said: “We are sick and tired of being sick and tired. They didn’t seem very engaged, but I was wrong. They showed up.”

Republicans ran a scorched-earth campaign to paint Democrats as communists and branded El-Sayed a terrorist who would endanger Americans.

“You deserve to be able to see a doctor without getting a huge bill,” he told Michiganders on the eve of the vote, vowing to upend America’s divisive multi-billion-dollar for-profit medical system.

headline: Military facilities in Saudi Arabia targeted by drones and missiles: Houthi spokesperson
description: Houthi spokesperson Yahya Saree has announced that the group carried out multiple drone and missile attacks on...
article_text:
Houthi spokesperson Yahya Saree has announced that the group carried out multiple drone and missile attacks on military facilities within Saudi Arabia.

In a post on X, Saree says three attacks were carried out, with the first being a “direct” drone strike targeting a radar facility in the Al-Qahma Peninsula north of Jizan.

“The second operation targeted the Aakefah camp in Najran with a ballistic missile and successfully achieved its objective,” Saree adds.

He also says a ballistic missile targeted a command and control building of the Saudi Border Guard in Jizan, “resulting in dead and wounded among the soldiers and officers of the Saudi enemy”.

Houthi spokesperson Yahya Saree claims the strike was successful and caused “significant damage to the airport”.

In a post on X, he reiterates the group’s call to all airlines, staff and travellers to refrain from flying through Saudi airspace, “as it is not secure”.

headline: ‘I’ll be working for de-escalation,’ want Strait of Hormuz fully reopened: British PM
description: British Prime Minister Andy Burnham has promised to push for de-escalation in the Middle East following the...
article_text:
British Prime Minister Andy Burnham has promised to push for de-escalation in the Middle East following the Democrats’ victory in the US midterm elections, Al Jazeera reports.

Asked whether he thought the results would make President Donald Trump more unpredictable, the UK prime minister replies, “Trump has accepted the results, and I feel the world has an opportunity now to unite around the issue that is affecting us all, and that’s the cost of living.

“That has been the issue that I have put front and centre in my first three months in Downing Street, and we’ve made moves. But I can’t get people’s cost of living pressures down until the conflict in the Middle East is resolved.”

When asked if he is worried about a possible escalation in the Middle East following the results, he says “Well, I’ll be working for de-escalation to make it very clear. You know, we want to see a resolution, the Strait of Hormuz fully opened again.”

headline: ECP objects to retired SC judge's remarks about 2023 ruling on polls in Punjab and KP, reserved seats case
description: Says it is “unfortunate” that a retired judge is taking a position against the Constitution and the law.
author: News Desk
article_text:
The Election Commission of Pakistan (ECP) on Wednesday objected to remarks made by former senior puisne judge of the Supreme Court of Pakistan, Mansoor Ali Shah, regarding polls in KP and Punjab and the reserved seats case pertaining to the PTI.

Shah made the remarks at an event organised by the US-based Community Alliance for Peace and Justice on October 29, where he was asked about his dissenting opinion in the 2023 SC ruling on provincial elections in Punjab and KP and whether it was a “turning point” and the beginning of a “division” within the SC.

In its 3-2 verdict, the SC, after taking a suo motu notice, directed that elections should be held within 90 days in both provinces. Two judges, including Shah, had dissented from the ruling, saying that the suo motu proceedings initiated by then-chief justice of Pakistan Umar Ata Bandial, were “wholly unjustified”, besides being initiated with “undue haste”.

In their detailed reasoning, they explained that the SC by a majority of 4-3 and not 3-2 had dismissed the suo motu hearing on polls delay in Punjab and KP and therefore the same should be considered as the “Order of the Court”.

It had resulted in a controversy, with the government igniting a raging debate claiming that the ruling was a 4-3 majority decision in its favour and not a 3-2 verdict against.

In response to the question, Shah said that this was the time when the ex-chief justice was forming “like-minded benches”, adding that three or four judges were attending to the majority of the cases.

He said that initially the matter was taken by the high courts. He said that the SC judges had gathered in the ante-room and discussed with the chief justice at the time that suo motu notice should not be taken at this point. He said that it was “agreed” to wait but days later a SC bench took up the matter under suo motu powers as he denounced the “one-man show” going on at the time.

He said that at the time, two SC judges — Justice Yahya Afridi and Justice Athar Minallah — had dismissed the petitions in the case. He said that the SC bench was later reconstituted, adding that since two judges had decided the matter, the verdict could not be dismissed. He said that this sparked the 4-3, 2-3 debate.

In a statement on Wednesday, the ECP referred to the remarks made by Shah, saying that they ignored “basic constitutional and legal facts related to the election matters and judicial decisions”.

“It is highly inappropriate to present the judicial record for specific purposes through selective quotations, incomplete perspectives and one-sided interpretations,” the statement said.

The ECP also stated that according to Shah’s claims, the election ruling was a “minority decision” and the commission could not have held polls.

As a result, the commission said that the party’s election symbol was withdrawn, which, the ECP added, was also upheld by the SC in 2025, along with rejecting review petitions filed by the PTI.

The ECP further stated that PTI held intra-party elections after five years and its proceedings remained pending before the commission as the “PTI itself has taken a stay order from a high court”. It further stated that as per the commission’s records, the PTI was still enlisted as a political party.

The ECP added that only political parties which contested the elections had a right to the reserved seats.

It further stated that it was mandatory for a political party to win at least one seat and that independent members were not entitled to reserved seats and therefore, the ECP gave the seats to the eligible parties.

headline: PIA to run 3 weekly direct flights between Islamabad and Birmingham from Dec 1
description: Flights will initially operate on Tuesdays, Thursdays and Saturdays, airline says.
author: News Desk
article_text:
Pakistan International Airlines (PIA) announced on Wednesday that it is launching three weekly direct flights between Islamabad and Birmingham from Dec 1.

The new flights will initially operate on Tuesdays, Thursdays and Saturdays, according to a statement by the airline’s spokesperson. He added that the flights will provide direct air travel to a “large number of Pakistanis living in the northern and central regions of the United Kingdom (UK)”.

The statement added that the UK was a “highly important” air route for the airline, noting that efforts were being made to increase the total number of weekly flights between the country and Pakistan to 23.

In a post on X on Tuesday, Birmingham Airport said: “Due to high demand from travellers in the Midlands , direct flights to Islamabad will be resuming three times a week.”

In September, PIA said it would increase its weekly flights to London from four to seven, starting from Oct 27.

Pakistani flights had been banned from flying to the European Union, UK and United States in June 2020, after one of its aircraft crashed in Karachi, killing nearly 100 people on board.

The European Union Air Safety Agency had barred PIA from operating in EU countries over safety concerns. The ban on flights followed then-aviation minister Ghulam Sarwar Khan’s statement on the floor of parliament, where he termed pilots’ licences “dubious”.

headline: Democrats win US Congress in midterm rout of Trump
description: Vote reflects deep anger over living costs, tariffs and Trump's war against Iran, which has sent fuel prices soaring and compounded dissatisfaction with an already deeply unpopular president.
author: Reuters, AFP
article_text:
Democrats seized control of the US Congress on Wednesday, capturing the Senate and House of Representatives in a stunning, nationwide rejection of Donald Trump set to put the brakes on the final two years of his presidency.

The Democratic landslide will give the opposition power to block legislation, launch broad investigations into Trump’s administration and thwart his judicial and senior government appointments.

The vote reflected deep anger over living costs, tariffs and Trump’s war against Iran, which has sent fuel prices soaring and compounded dissatisfaction with an already deeply unpopular president.

Trump struck a conciliatory note despite his history of questioning election results, telling The New York Times: “I am absolutely willing to accept those results” and promising to “work with the Democrats”.

“I think the Democrats did a good job, I really do,” the 80-year-old told Fox News, in rare praise for his political opponents. “They fought hard.”

But he sought to distance himself from his own party’s poor showing, adding: “I don’t view it as a hit on me.”

He acknowledged that the Iran conflict had contributed to the defeat but defended the military campaign, and he suggested the rival parties could find common ground on immigration, long one of the most divisive issues of his presidency.

But minutes later on social media the 80-year-old signalled how he intends to deal with Democratic attempts to pass laws, posting a picture of a red baseball cap emblazoned: “VETO.”

The Democrats’ decisive Senate breakthroughs came in Kansas and Iowa, the fifth and sixth Republican-held seats to fall in the extraordinary “blue wave” election night.

In Kansas, Methodist minister Adam Hamilton defeated Republican incumbent Roger Marshall, becoming the first Democrat elected to the Senate from the reliably conservative state since 1932.

Iowa had not elected a Democratic senator since 2008, again illustrating the scale of party’s inroads into Republican strongholds.

The upsets followed victories in Texas, South Carolina, North Carolina and Ohio, where voters rejected Republican candidates despite Trump’s intensive efforts to rally his supporters.

Democrat James Talarico ousted a Trump-backed Senate candidate, while Gina Hinojosa unseated Republican governor Greg Abbott, ending decades of Republican control of the state’s top office.

Talarico said that “we defeated Goliath” after winning a US Senate seat over Texas attorney General Ken Paxton, a close ally of President Donald Trump who was heavily backed by tech billionaire Elon Musk.

“In this race, we went up against our own Goliaths. The richest man in the world, the most powerful man in the world, and the entire Washington, DC establishment,” Talarico told a victory rally in the Texas capital, Austin.

Democrats also protected key Senate seats of their own, including Jon Ossoff’s in Georgia and an open seat in New Hampshire.

In California, Democrat Xavier Becerra handily defeated Donald Trump-backed Republican Steve Hilton in the race to become the governor, US networks said.

Partial results showed Becerra, a career politician who served in the cabinet of former president Joe Biden, had a nearly two-to-one advantage over Hilton, with about half of the ballots counted.

Becerra had run a low-key campaign in a state where Democrats heavily outnumber Republicans and where the Trump brand is almost toxic.

The son of Mexican immigrants, he will be the first elected Latino governor of California, a state that would be the world’s fourth-largest economy if it were a country.

“Ladies and gentlemen, you have now entered the Becerra era,” the former US Health and Human Services secretary told his supporters at a victory party in Sacramento.

“I didn’t run to make history,” he said. “I ran to make a difference for anyone and everyone who calls California home, whether you voted for me or not.”

Becerra will replace term-limited Governor Gavin Newsom, a Democratic Party big-hitter who is believed to have his eyes on a tilt at the White House in 2028.

Hilton, a British-born conservative former pundit who was once an adviser to former UK prime minister David Cameron, had always been a long shot.

He conceded he had lost a difficult race.

“Maybe this isn’t the best year to be running for office as a Republican when we see what’s going on around the country,” he said.

Republicans had held a 53-47 Senate majority.

The six-seat Democratic gain proved sufficient for networks to project a takeover despite some races remaining unresolved.

Republican heartland

Democrats also captured the House after flipping Republican-held districts in states stretching from Pennsylvania and New Jersey to Kentucky, Arizona and North Carolina.

Some victories came in territory Trump had carried comfortably in 2024, despite Republican attempts to shore up House seats by redrawing electoral boundaries.

One bellwether was Indiana, where Democrat J.D. Ford defeated Republican congresswoman Victoria Spartz in a district Trump won by 17 points. Analysts had identified an upset there as a warning of a much wider Democratic advance.

In Georgia, former Atlanta mayor Keisha Lance Bottoms became the first Black woman elected governor in US history, while other Democratic gains extended to statehouses across the country.

Republicans had some bright spots in Florida, where Trump-backed Byron Donalds won the governorship, becoming the state’s first Black governor, and Ashley Moody kept a Senate seat.

George Washington University professor Todd Belt called the Democratic advance “a big wipeout and a strong repudiation of Donald Trump and his policies,” citing voters’ concerns about the economy, corruption and the Iran conflict.

Trump on defensive

Democrats will now be able to block Trump’s legislation, investigate his administration over corruption allegations, the Iran war and immigration enforcement, and use Senate control to thwart judicial appointments and senior nominations.

Robert Garcia, a Democrat expected to lead the powerful House Oversight Committee, warned Republicans on social media: “LAWYER UP.”

House Democratic leader Hakeem Jeffries declared Trump’s MAGA movement “on the run from sea to shining sea.”

Jeffries is also positioned to become the first Black speaker of the House when the new Congress convenes in January, if elected by his colleagues.

As speaker, Jeffries, representing a New York City congressional district, would preside over a majority that will be sworn in the first week of January, taking the reins from Republicans who controlled the House for the past four years.

“Today begins the great American comeback,” Jeffries proclaimed in a victory speech late on Tuesday after media outlets projected the likelihood of Democratic majorities in the House and Senate.

For many voters, the central concern was Trump’s stewardship of the economy.

“Rent, groceries, utility bills, and property taxes keep climbing,” 24-year-old Los Angeles voter Taylor Cook told AFP.

A rebuke to Trump, winner says

“In sweeping and decisive victories, the American people have rebuked the depravity, corruption and incompetence of the man named President Donald J. Trump,” incumbent Democratic Senator Jon Ossoff, the projected winner in Georgia, told supporters at a victory party.

In Florida, Republican Senator Ashley Moody fended off Democrat Angie Nixon but was ahead by only about three percentage points in a state Trump carried by 13 points in 2024, according to a vote count compiled by Reuters and USA Today, further evidence that even solidly Republican states were shifting dramatically toward Democrats.

Democrats held onto three House districts in Florida that Republican lawmakers had redrawn earlier this year, all of which backed Trump by at least nine percentage points, according to media projections.

Democrat Keisha Lance Bottoms, a former mayor of Atlanta, on Tuesday was elected governor of the state of Georgia, becoming the first Black woman elected to that office in the US, media projections showed.

CNN and NBC News called the race in her favour.

Bottoms defeated billionaire health care executive Rick Jackson, who ran as a Republican. Current Governor Brian Kemp is term-limited and could not run again.

Midterm elections are typically viewed as a referendum on the president, and that is especially true for Trump, who dominates attention like no other politician. Trump himself told his supporters to “pretend I’m on the ballot” and held dozens of rallies in the closing weeks.

According to exit polls conducted by SSRS on behalf of a consortium of US media outlets, including major television networks and the Associated Press, half of voters nationwide said they saw the 2026 midterm elections as an opportunity to rebuke the president, and three-quarters said they are “angry” or “dissatisfied” with the way the country is headed.

In addition, 70 per cent of voters surveyed said they want Congress to provide more checks and balances on the president.

History is against Republicans: the sitting president’s party has lost ground in Congress in all but two midterms since World War Two. Trump’s approval rating is hovering near his career lows, with voters frustrated by war on Iran, higher fuel prices and wider affordability concerns.

Led by Trump, Republicans have portrayed Democratic candidates as radical, un-American and even communist, labels Democrats flatly reject.

Opinion polls show voters are most concerned about affordability and disapprove of Trump’s handling of the issue. His tariffs on imports, many of which the courts threw out, and his decision to attack Iran in February raised prices for consumers.

Trump deploys election monitors

The US Justice Department said it had deployed 1,000 election monitors and observers to all 50 states in what it called the largest Election Day monitoring effort in history.

Democrats criticised the plan as potential voter intimidation. In roughly two-thirds of the jurisdictions the department listed, voters supported Democrat Kamala Harris over Trump in the 2024 presidential election, a Reuters analysis found.

Election officials in several states reported no issues with the monitoring effort. New Mexico’s secretary of state’s office said it had received reports of federal monitors asking “unusual questions” in one county and that the Justice Department offered assurances that the conduct would be addressed.

article_html:
Democrats seized control of the US Congress on Wednesday, capturing the Senate and House of Representatives in a stunning, nationwide rejection of Donald Trump set to put the brakes on the final two years of his presidency.

The Democratic landslide will give the opposition power to block legislation, launch broad investigations into Trump’s administration and thwart his judicial and senior government appointments.

The vote reflected deep anger over living costs, tariffs and Trump’s war against Iran, which has sent fuel prices soaring and compounded dissatisfaction with an already deeply unpopular president.

Trump struck a conciliatory note despite his history of questioning election results, telling The New York Times: “I am absolutely willing to accept those results” and promising to “work with the Democrats”.

“I think the Democrats did a good job, I really do,” the 80-year-old told Fox News, in rare praise for his political opponents. “They fought hard.”

But he sought to distance himself from his own party’s poor showing, adding: “I don’t view it as a hit on me.”

He acknowledged that the Iran conflict had contributed to the defeat but defended the military campaign, and he suggested the rival parties could find common ground on immigration, long one of the most divisive issues of his presidency.

But minutes later on social media the 80-year-old signalled how he intends to deal with Democratic attempts to pass laws, posting a picture of a red baseball cap emblazoned: “VETO.”

The Democrats’ decisive Senate breakthroughs came in Kansas and Iowa, the fifth and sixth Republican-held seats to fall in the extraordinary “blue wave” election night.

In Kansas, Methodist minister Adam Hamilton defeated Republican incumbent Roger Marshall, becoming the first Democrat elected to the Senate from the reliably conservative state since 1932.

Iowa had not elected a Democratic senator since 2008, again illustrating the scale of party’s inroads into Republican strongholds.

The upsets followed victories in Texas, South Carolina, North Carolina and Ohio, where voters rejected Republican candidates despite Trump’s intensive efforts to rally his supporters.

Democrat James Talarico ousted a Trump-backed Senate candidate, while Gina Hinojosa unseated Republican governor Greg Abbott, ending decades of Republican control of the state’s top office.

Talarico said that “we defeated Goliath” after winning a US Senate seat over Texas attorney General Ken Paxton, a close ally of President Donald Trump who was heavily backed by tech billionaire Elon Musk.

“In this race, we went up against our own Goliaths. The richest man in the world, the most powerful man in the world, and the entire Washington, DC establishment,” Talarico told a victory rally in the Texas capital, Austin.

Democrats also protected key Senate seats of their own, including Jon Ossoff’s in Georgia and an open seat in New Hampshire.

In California, Democrat Xavier Becerra handily defeated Donald Trump-backed Republican Steve Hilton in the race to become the governor, US networks said.

Partial results showed Becerra, a career politician who served in the cabinet of former president Joe Biden, had a nearly two-to-one advantage over Hilton, with about half of the ballots counted.

Becerra had run a low-key campaign in a state where Democrats heavily outnumber Republicans and where the Trump brand is almost toxic.

The son of Mexican immigrants, he will be the first elected Latino governor of California, a state that would be the world’s fourth-largest economy if it were a country.

“Ladies and gentlemen, you have now entered the Becerra era,” the former US Health and Human Services secretary told his supporters at a victory party in Sacramento.

“I didn’t run to make history,” he said. “I ran to make a difference for anyone and everyone who calls California home, whether you voted for me or not.”

Becerra will replace term-limited Governor Gavin Newsom, a Democratic Party big-hitter who is believed to have his eyes on a tilt at the White House in 2028.

Hilton, a British-born conservative former pundit who was once an adviser to former UK prime minister David Cameron, had always been a long shot.

He conceded he had lost a difficult race.

“Maybe this isn’t the best year to be running for office as a Republican when we see what’s going on around the country,” he said.

Republicans had held a 53-47 Senate majority.

The six-seat Democratic gain proved sufficient for networks to project a takeover despite some races remaining unresolved.

Republican heartland

Democrats also captured the House after flipping Republican-held districts in states stretching from Pennsylvania and New Jersey to Kentucky, Arizona and North Carolina.

Some victories came in territory Trump had carried comfortably in 2024, despite Republican attempts to shore up House seats by redrawing electoral boundaries.

One bellwether was Indiana, where Democrat J.D. Ford defeated Republican congresswoman Victoria Spartz in a district Trump won by 17 points. Analysts had identified an upset there as a warning of a much wider Democratic advance.

In Georgia, former Atlanta mayor Keisha Lance Bottoms became the first Black woman elected governor in US history, while other Democratic gains extended to statehouses across the country.

Republicans had some bright spots in Florida, where Trump-backed Byron Donalds won the governorship, becoming the state’s first Black governor, and Ashley Moody kept a Senate seat.

George Washington University professor Todd Belt called the Democratic advance “a big wipeout and a strong repudiation of Donald Trump and his policies,” citing voters’ concerns about the economy, corruption and the Iran conflict.

Trump on defensive

Democrats will now be able to block Trump’s legislation, investigate his administration over corruption allegations, the Iran war and immigration enforcement, and use Senate control to thwart judicial appointments and senior nominations.

Robert Garcia, a Democrat expected to lead the powerful House Oversight Committee, warned Republicans on social media: “LAWYER UP.”

House Democratic leader Hakeem Jeffries declared Trump’s MAGA movement “on the run from sea to shining sea.”

Jeffries is also positioned to become the first Black speaker of the House when the new Congress convenes in January, if elected by his colleagues.

As speaker, Jeffries, representing a New York City congressional district, would preside over a majority that will be sworn in the first week of January, taking the reins from Republicans who controlled the House for the past four years.

“Today begins the great American comeback,” Jeffries proclaimed in a victory speech late on Tuesday after media outlets projected the likelihood of Democratic majorities in the House and Senate.

For many voters, the central concern was Trump’s stewardship of the economy.

“Rent, groceries, utility bills, and property taxes keep climbing,” 24-year-old Los Angeles voter Taylor Cook told AFP.

A rebuke to Trump, winner says

“In sweeping and decisive victories, the American people have rebuked the depravity, corruption and incompetence of the man named President Donald J. Trump,” incumbent Democratic Senator Jon Ossoff, the projected winner in Georgia, told supporters at a victory party.

In Florida, Republican Senator Ashley Moody fended off Democrat Angie Nixon but was ahead by only about three percentage points in a state Trump carried by 13 points in 2024, according to a vote count compiled by Reuters and USA Today, further evidence that even solidly Republican states were shifting dramatically toward Democrats.

Democrats held onto three House districts in Florida that Republican lawmakers had redrawn earlier this year, all of which backed Trump by at least nine percentage points, according to media projections.

Democrat Keisha Lance Bottoms, a former mayor of Atlanta, on Tuesday was elected governor of the state of Georgia, becoming the first Black woman elected to that office in the US, media projections showed.

CNN and NBC News called the race in her favour.

Bottoms defeated billionaire health care executive Rick Jackson, who ran as a Republican. Current Governor Brian Kemp is term-limited and could not run again.

Midterm elections are typically viewed as a referendum on the president, and that is especially true for Trump, who dominates attention like no other politician. Trump himself told his supporters to “pretend I’m on the ballot” and held dozens of rallies in the closing weeks.

According to exit polls conducted by SSRS on behalf of a consortium of US media outlets, including major television networks and the Associated Press, half of voters nationwide said they saw the 2026 midterm elections as an opportunity to rebuke the president, and three-quarters said they are “angry” or “dissatisfied” with the way the country is headed.

In addition, 70 per cent of voters surveyed said they want Congress to provide more checks and balances on the president.

History is against Republicans: the sitting president’s party has lost ground in Congress in all but two midterms since World War Two. Trump’s approval rating is hovering near his career lows, with voters frustrated by war on Iran, higher fuel prices and wider affordability concerns.

Led by Trump, Republicans have portrayed Democratic candidates as radical, un-American and even communist, labels Democrats flatly reject.

Opinion polls show voters are most concerned about affordability and disapprove of Trump’s handling of the issue. His tariffs on imports, many of which the courts threw out, and his decision to attack Iran in February raised prices for consumers.

Trump deploys election monitors

The US Justice Department said it had deployed 1,000 election monitors and observers to all 50 states in what it called the largest Election Day monitoring effort in history.

Democrats criticised the plan as potential voter intimidation. In roughly two-thirds of the jurisdictions the department listed, voters supported Democrat Kamala Harris over Trump in the 2024 presidential election, a Reuters analysis found.

Election officials in several states reported no issues with the monitoring effort. New Mexico’s secretary of state’s office said it had received reports of federal monitors asking “unusual questions” in one county and that the Justice Department offered assurances that the conduct would be addressed.

House Democratic leader Hakeem Jeffries declared Trump’s MAGA movement “on the run from sea to shining sea.”
Jeffries is also positioned to become the first Black speaker of the House when the new Congress convenes in January, if elected by his colleagues.

As speaker, Jeffries, representing a New York City congressional district, would preside over a majority that will be sworn in the first week of January, taking the reins from Republicans who controlled the House for the past four years.
“Today begins the great American comeback,” Jeffries proclaimed in a victory speech late on Tuesday after media outlets projected the likelihood of Democratic majorities in the House and Senate.
For many voters, the central concern was Trump’s stewardship of the economy.
“Rent, groceries, utility bills, and property taxes keep climbing,” 24-year-old Los Angeles voter Taylor Cook told AFP.
A rebuke to Trump, winner says

“In sweeping and decisive victories, the American people have rebuked the depravity, corruption and incompetence of the man named President Donald J. Trump,” incumbent Democratic Senator Jon Ossoff, the projected winner in Georgia, told supporters at a victory party.

In Florida, Republican Senator Ashley Moody fended off Democrat Angie Nixon but was ahead by only about three percentage points in a state Trump carried by 13 points in 2024, according to a vote count compiled by Reuters and USA Today, further evidence that even solidly Republican states were shifting dramatically toward Democrats.

Democrats held onto three House districts in Florida that Republican lawmakers had redrawn earlier this year, all of which backed Trump by at least nine percentage points, according to media projections.

Democrat Keisha Lance Bottoms, a former mayor of Atlanta, on Tuesday was elected governor of the state of Georgia, becoming the first Black woman elected to that office in the US, media projections showed.
CNN and NBC News called the race in her favour.
Bottoms defeated billionaire health care executive Rick Jackson, who ran as a Republican. Current Governor Brian Kemp is term-limited and could not run again.

Midterm elections are typically viewed as a referendum on the president, and that is especially true for Trump, who dominates attention like no other politician. Trump himself told his supporters to “pretend I’m on the ballot” and held dozens of rallies in the closing weeks.

According to exit polls conducted by SSRS on behalf of a consortium of US media outlets, including major television networks and the Associated Press, half of voters nationwide said they saw the 2026 midterm elections as an opportunity to rebuke the president, and three-quarters said they are “angry” or “dissatisfied” with the way the country is headed.
In addition, 70 per cent of voters surveyed said they want Congress to provide more checks and balances on the president.

History is against Republicans: the sitting president’s party has lost ground in Congress in all but two midterms since World War Two. Trump’s approval rating is hovering near his career lows, with voters frustrated by war on Iran, higher fuel prices and wider affordability concerns.
Led by Trump, Republicans have portrayed Democratic candidates as radical, un-American and even communist, labels Democrats flatly reject.

Opinion polls show voters are most concerned about affordability and disapprove of Trump’s handling of the issue. His tariffs on imports, many of which the courts threw out, and his decision to attack Iran in February raised prices for consumers.
Trump deploys election monitors
The US Justice Department said it had deployed 1,000 election monitors and observers to all 50 states in what it called the largest Election Day monitoring effort in history.

Democrats criticised the plan as potential voter intimidation. In roughly two-thirds of the jurisdictions the department listed, voters supported Democrat Kamala Harris over Trump in the 2024 presidential election, a Reuters analysis found.

Election officials in several states reported no issues with the monitoring effort. New Mexico’s secretary of state’s office said it had received reports of federal monitors asking “unusual questions” in one county and that the Justice Department offered assurances that the conduct would be addressed.

headline: 'The reason we lost is the war': JD Vance acknowledges Iran conflict made supporters abandon Trump
description: US Vice President JD Vance has commented on the midterm results that have been a blow to his Republican party,...
article_text:
US Vice President JD Vance has commented on the midterm results that have been a blow to his Republican party, saying the “real reason we lost is obvious to almost everyone”.

“The reason we lost is the war. The president himself said so last night,” he wrote in a lengthy post on X.

He said in a poll conducted by a pollster, “a lot of Trump 2024 voters were angry and planning to vote for Democrats”.

“He asked those voters who had abandoned us what would cause them to come back on our team. The top four answers, accounting for nearly all of the responses were:

End the war
Focus on cost of living/inflation
Put America First
Change our relationship to Israel”
